utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, good morning, everyone. Although we have witness and his counsel in the courtroom, there are a couple of matters I'd like to deal with before we continue with witness's evidence. The Chamber will first turn to a statement made by the Prosecution on the 8th of April, 2013, during the testimony of Soniboje Skiljevic in relation to scheduled incident C.18.2 (KP Dom Butmir). In response to a document made by the Chamber as to the time-frame of the charges related to KP Dom, the Prosecution stated that it had extended the time period that it initially alleged for the operation of KP Dom and referred to a footnote in the indictment. Here I refer to transcript page 36774. The Chamber notes that Schedule C.18.2 pertains to the cruel and inhumane treatment related -- yes, inhumane treatment related charges at KP Dom Butmir and specifically refers to "May until October 1992." Footnote 12 of the indictment linked to Schedule C.18.2 reads: "The KP Dom Butmir detention facility (Kula prison) served as a detention facility until at least 28th of October, 1994." The Chamber considers that the duration of the operation of the KP Dom Butmir is different from the temporal scope of the crimes alleged to have occurred there and in relation to which the accused is charged. The temporal scope of the relevant crimes charged is clearly identified in scheduled incident C.18.2 as "May to October 1992." Therefore, the Chamber considers that only findings on the cruel and inhumane treatment related charges at KP Dom Butmir in this specific time period may be entered into. I would also refer to pages 52 to 54 of Appendix B of the Prosecution's Rule 73 bis submissions filed on the 31st of August, 2009. In relation to the crime of forced labour which is charged in paragraph 60(h) of the indictment, the Chamber notes that paragraph 60(h) of the indictment does not make a specific reference to Schedule C and that the Prosecution's 73 bis submissions does not limit the time-frame for the forced labour charge in the municipality relevant to the KP Dom Butmir. The Chamber is therefore of the view that the forced labour charge extends throughout the existence of KP Dom. Next, the Chamber notes the submission filed by the Registry on the 26th of April, 2013, in relation to the Chamber's decisions of 22nd March 2013, and the 19th of April, 2013, in which the Registry was ordered to disclose, for an in camera inspection by the Chamber, copies of "any reports or information on the psychological state of Milan Babic." In its latest submission, the Registry submits that the medical officer at the UNDU, having reviewed Milan Babic's medical file, found no "psychological or psychiatric records." The Chamber once again refers to the report on the death of Milan Babic issued by Judge Parker in 2006. It is clear from that report that Milan Babic had several medical consultations, including psychological and psychiatric evaluations during his stay at the UNDU. For example, Judge Parker refers to a psychological evaluation conducted on the 5th of March, 2004, at the request of OLAD as well as the fact that Milan Babic was examined and his mental state assessed by the medical officer upon his arrival to UNDU on the 7th of February, 2006. Finally, the report states that Milan Babic saw the UNDU psychiatrist, who is based mainly in Belgrade, just before his transfer to a third state. Admittedly, Judge Parker also stated that the psychiatric records were not kept discounting Milan Babic's psychiatric records -- I'm sorry. Admittedly, Judge Parker also stated that the psychiatric records were not kept at the UNDU but were in the psychiatrist's custody. Nevertheless, even discounting Milan Babic's psychiatric records, it thus appears that other evaluations of Milan Babic's psychological state were made by the UNDU medical officers during his stay at the UNDU. The Chamber finds it incomprehensible that these were either never recorded in Milan Babic's medical file or now cannot be found. Accordingly, it orders the Registry to file another submission addressing this issue. Finally, noting the Registry's submission, the Chamber is concerned that the medical officer at the UNDU may be interpreting the Chamber's order too narrowly. Accordingly, it instructs the Registry to liaise with the medical officer and to emphasise to him that the Chamber's order was to disclose "copies of any reports or information on the psychological state of Milan Babic." I emphasise again "any reports or information." These shall include also those records which provide that Milan Babic's psychological state is fine, which appears to have been the case following Babic's examination on the 7th of February, 2006. The said submission addressing all of these issues and reporting on the Registry's consultations with the UNDU medical officer shall be filed by the close of business on the 9th of May, 2013. Should any reports or information on the psychological state of Milan Babic be located during the preparation of said submission, the Registry shall disclose them to the Chamber immediately. That said, unless there's any other issues to be raised, we'll continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have a small follow-up on something Your Honours raised during our last week with you, and that was with respect to whether the parties could agree between themselves on translations of a map of Sarajevo so that Your Honours would have English translations of unit designations. And what we've been able to agree on, Your Honours, is translations of the unit designations in P1021 and the translated version of that map is now available in e-court as 65 ter number 11789I, capital I, and translations of D718, which is a -- D718 is a magnified cutout of Sarajevo from P1021, and so to have the fullest possible amount of designations translated we dealt with that one as well, and that's been uploaded as 65 ter number 13636B. And with Mr. Robinson's agreement, I wonder if we could move those in for submission at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We agree and appreciate the work that the Prosecution did on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibits P6295 and P6296 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Prosecutor. I apologise. I failed to turn on my microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not a problem, General. I'd like to begin today, General, by looking -- going directly to a document that you signed on 15 November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's 65 ter number 24986, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document -- actually, it's dated 17 November 1992, referring to a meeting on 15 November 1992. It sets out the conclusions and tasks from a symposium --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to say hello to you all first of all. Last time I had asked you to provide me with a hard copy, courtesy copy, of these documents so that I can follow them, whatever language they are in. I realise that this hasn't been done. If I could have the entire text, please, and that would be something I would appreciate greatly. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, are you not following the document in front of you with -- and -- if you could expand further on the necessity that you have to see these documents while the cross-examination is going on and the basis as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. If, for instance, we were to take this document, I can only see one paragraph or two paragraphs of this document. I think this is an excellent rule between colleagues to provide the documents a little bit ahead of time as matter of courtesy, and if there is a problem, I would like to be able to see it ahead of time. It's just a matter of courtesy. This is how things are done in honour -- in other bars around the world. I don't see why we should not abide by this rule. It's just a question of disclosing them. It's just a matter of having the entire document to be able to pre-empt any problem, potential problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can put that way, your client is not an accused in this case but is giving evidence. I wonder whether every witness is being provided with documents that is going to be shown to him in advance, but I'd like to hear from the parties as to the submission or request of Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I'll just stand by what I said last time when Mr. Piletta-Zanin raised this. I invited him to address his concern to Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President. We think that -- we recognise there's probably no right to the information, but as a matter of courtesy if the Prosecution -- we have these documents in e-court, but Mr. Piletta-Zanin doesn't have access to the e-court for this case, so if the Prosecution could compile hard copies of the documents it's going to use during its cross-examination and provide a set to Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that would be a very nice thing to do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I almost couldn't see you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It seems that we're going in circles. This was raised before previously, and as Mr. Robinson is aware, the Prosecution -- and as the Chamber is aware, Prosecution consistently does everything within its power to accommodate the needs of all parties. As Ms. Edgerton noted to the Court the other day, the additional burden would be significant in this case. I think the Court hit the nail on the head in identifying the difference between an accused and disclosure of those informations and a witness who does not receive the materials before or contemporaneous with the commencement of the cross-examination. In fact, as we know, it's -- Mr. Galic who is being cross-examined is a witness in this case. If he has an issue with his comprehension of a document in context, he can and has asked for the opportunity to scroll down and see further. And as the Court is well aware, it has not been the practice in this case nor has it been the practice in any case in which I've been involved for the documents during cross-examination to be provided to counsel representing that witness. So I -- I'm repeating basically what was said before, but I think the Court's previous position on this matter was sound, and we've not heard anything that should change that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like to add anything, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly. I understood that the burden would be too heavy for the Prosecution. I'm prepared to help the accused [as interpreted] and finance it myself to have a few copies, just 30 copies -- 30 seconds before the witness's examination. If it's too much to ask, then I shall withdraw my request, but I had hoped we would be on the same wavelength.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Line 1, page 8, instead of "I'm prepared to help the accused," please read "I'm prepared to help the Prosecution."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber finds that the request of Mr. Piletta-Zanin is not warranted in the circumstances, and if the witness is not able to understand the question, he can ask clarification with the Prosecution. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, you've actually had the first page of this document in front of you for quite a while now because of that intervention. I'd just like to have us flip over to page 4 of the document, the last page, so that you can see. Is that your signature on the document, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. So if we could go back over to page 1. This is -- sets out, as far as I can see from the document, the conclusions and tasks from a symposium on the military and political situation in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps together with your staff, local municipality presidents, brigade commanders, General Mladic, and General Tolimir, among others; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go over in both documents to English page 2 and B/C/S page 2, paragraph 1. Under the -- under the heading "Tasks," we see the following: 1 --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we please zoom in as I cannot see it and follow the document in this way. My glasses are not good enough -- or, rather, they are, but my eyes are not good enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No problem. Launching persistent -- among the tasks are launching persistent and crucial defence along the reached lines, particularly in the Sarajevo region, defending the territory of the Republika Srpska, observing the unconditional cease-fire, providing that the "Poturice" do the same, manoeuvring forces, firepower, and timely redeploying forces to improve the operational position of the corps forces. And then after that a number of offensive tasks are listed, and they're listed to start, as we see, if we go over to the next page, on 18 November 1992. So I have a question about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page only for the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For the English, yes. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, during your testimony in chief, His Honour Judge Kwon at page 37580 asked you what the word "Poturice" meant because it was used in a document signed by your Chief of Staff, and you said that it's a derogatory word for Muslims and that it was not a term that you would use, but you've actually used it in this document, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's obviously in the document, but the question is who wrote the document? I did approve it. It's a question whether I wrote it. But it was the usual thing to use that term. Then called us the Chetniks. We called them "Poturice" or others. The Ustashas. That was the way people communicated at the time. Though I still stand by what I said, namely that the term "Poturice" is a term which is not acceptable, at least not in this time. Perhaps at that time it was like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you told His Honour Judge Kwon that you would never use the word, that was incorrect, wasn't it? You've used it here.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never said that, but as far as I remember, I said that this is not the way I would express myself, rather than never. "Never" is a heavy word to be used, especially under the circumstances of a civil and inter-religious war. That is a term that was quite frequently used in mutual communication and so on. As I say, later on when I moved -- you have to realise that this was a moment when I just had arrived. I had many problems. That was only a month after my arrival in the corps. So I did not manage to have the corps under my control, if I can put it that way, let alone control what was written and how. What I said is that this is not the usual term that I would use, "Poturice," even though I may have used it occasionally. I cannot exclude that as a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this document as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6297, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, you actually continued to use that word, "Poturice," in describing the opposing forces, and you used that word in your reports to the Main Staff, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I don't know what are all the words that were used in reports within a two-year period. I cannot remember whether the word "Poturice" or Muslim armed forces or the BH Army or whatever it was called was used, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have not answered yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said "it's possible" at the beginning of your answer, General, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me him finish the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we discussed this document, you intervened several times that I didn't sign this document, but I did sign it, and I have confirmed it. There is no dilemma about it. But we said that these were reports or documents written by the corps command not personally by the commander, even though I was the one who signed them. I always signed and there is my signature in the end, whether it was me as the Chief of Staff or someone who was authorised to sign the document. As for the term itself, as I said, a new Chief of Staff arrived then. It's possible that he drew up such documents, and it's possible that I used it. Right now I cannot even remember that, whether that was a usual word for me at the time. I don't think so, but even if I did use it, there is nothing so special about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. What we'll do, General, then, is we'll go on to another topic that we began with actually last week, and it's the subject of protests. We were discussing it, actually, when we broke off, and maybe I'll see if we can come at it another way. Maybe I could ask you to confirm this: During your tour as commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, you were informed that shelling and sniping by your forces into Bosnian-held Sarajevo caused civilian casualties; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did receive such information as well, information.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, you received that information a number of ways, and you've talked about some of those, so let's see if I can get you to confirm that. You received that information through your staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Naturally through the staff, because that is the organ that works on all questions related to combat readiness, including this kind of information, what can be observed, perceived.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you also received that through Major Indjic; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you received that information verbally. For example, in meetings, conversations; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I've already stated that. At meetings I had with representatives of UNPROFOR, military observers, these questions were raised as well, so this is nothing new. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that information came to your corps and you in writing and in telephone calls, among other things; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already answered those questions as well if you remember, madam. Telephone? No, I did not receive such information by telephone. I don't speak English. They probably sent it down there to Indjic's office. As for written protests, we had some of those here, and we discussed them during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You received that information as well through the media; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you remember, we discussed a document here that had to do with this incident on the 4th of February, 1992. On the basis of media reports we found out about this, so we did find out. I said that I personally could not and did not have enough time to follow the media, and I couldn't have. I couldn't have because there was no electricity, and there were no other resources for doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- but you said, General, at transcript page 37397: "If we learned of an incident -- if we learned an incident did occur in various ways, whether through the media or whether because of a protest note or because we were informed through the Main Staff ..." So that seems to say that, as I just put to you, you did receive information not only through the media. You received it in writing, and, actually, you also added there you received information about shelling and sniping from the Main Staff as well, from the top down; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we speak that way using that kind of vocabulary, then it's a bit difficult to answer such questions. Now why is that the case? As for sniping and shelling, that means criminal activity, not legal military activity, and in Sarajevo and in that area there was a war that was going on for two years while I was commander, and we discussed that. We said there were civilian areas and there were military areas, that there were military targets. There are no civilian targets, because one is not allowed to engage civilian targets. So -- I do apologise. Sorry. Sorry, about that. I just needed to catch my breath. So when you say "sniping," I'll tell you, even in my judgement says that I was not accused of or convicted for sniping. It is footnote 711 of paragraph 254. However, I would like to underline once again that shelling that is referred to, mostly shelling as criminal activity, it primarily refers to mortar activity, so it's a mortar that fires -- so there's a bit of a lack of understanding there. So now when you ask me that way, you know, it is hard for me to say whether it is correct or not. You see, I don't know if I've been clear enough. I can give you an answer. I've come here to tell the truth, and there's no problem. Let us work on this together, and let us reach the truth this way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 7 -- or, rather, line 8, it is not reflected that the General said a mortar does not fire a shell but a mortar shell. [In English] So it's a mortar that fires. Mines, not grenades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And we're going to come back to your own reference to the trial judgement in your case, but rather than have my question disappear in some formalistic discussion, I want to go back to what you said when I first started to speak with you about protests. And my question to you was whether you could confirm that during your tour as commander of the SRK you were informed that shelling and sniping by your forces into Bosnian-held Sarajevo caused civilian casualties, and you said yes, you could confirm that you received that information. So are you now qualifying the answer that you just gave? Did you receive information or didn't you, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we are repeating ourselves several times with regard to the same question. I've given quite a few answers during the examination-in-chief and now with regard to these problems. Now, whether I received this information. During the examination-in-chief, documents of the corps command were displayed, and these documents show that we did receive such information. So there's no dilemma there whether we did receive this or not. However, you have to understand this other thing here, and I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to understand me on this as well. I want to say that when we looked at individual incidents, say, involving snipers, those that President Karadzic has been accused of, we have seen that we have -- that I had not received any protest for any one of these incidents. There's no trace of that for that day for that incident specifically, say, sniping activity. That's what you call it -- or, rather, that's what the Prosecution calls it and the Court accepted that. So whenever -- we have already explained what snipers are. There's a bit of confusion there. Not everything is sniping. That is why there's this ambiguity and then it's easy to manipulate that kind of thing. I think that we should be more decided on various matters, also including shelling including mortar shelling, mortar fire. These five incidents that are in my indictment and Mr. Karadzic's indictment, we said that -- now, when did I receive such information and where was I and what were the conditions involved and what I did. There's no dilemma there. That has already been discussed --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I have already presented --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, whether or not you personally received reports that these incidents had occurred is actually irrelevant, isn't it? You were the commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the commander, but such reports were being sent. We've already said that with regard to each and every incident -- or, rather, problem, this was recorded in the daily reports for the Main Staff. We would not have concealed something that happened. We did write something. We didn't write something else. That's impossible. Why would we do that? How would we do that? We wrote what we knew, and what we didn't -- oh, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, you gave evidence during your testimony in chief saying that as commander, you were -- and I'll be able to find the cite in a moment, you were six levels up the command chain, and you would not expect to receive a report of infantry fire being opened against an individual. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I think that you quite properly interpreted what I said. I agree with that. I said that I was some sixth level of command and control, and I did not receive all information. I could not have known of all incidents, whether they had happened or not happened. All of that is correct. There's no dilemma there. We did say that the front of the corps changed. However, if the average was 250 kilometres, well, just think of that. 250 kilometres. Does the commander know each and every detail? No, and there's no way he can. That is why such information was received by other levels of command too. But I'm speaking about specific incidents, and that's why I came here in a way to explain that part, those that President Karadzic has been accused of. And I was accused of that, too, and I was convicted, and you asked me. Now, how, in which way, and so on, I wouldn't want to go into that now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am afraid that it's going to remain that way, but on page 15, from lines 22 to 24, the General said that that's not reflected in the transcript, that the Prosecution accepted that every infantry fire is sniping, and he is indicating that now. And now from the repeated question of Madam Edgerton, we see that her understanding was that this is infantry fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it has been reflected in the sentence, I quote: "Not everything is sniping." But thank you anyway. Let's continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe we can go back to the very original question I asked, and it's about the information you received. Can you confirm that you received information from the Main Staff that shelling and sniping by your forces was causing casualties in Bosnian-held Sarajevo? Can you confirm that, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I personally receive this from the Main Staff, such information? I don't remember any such information, but had such information been sent along the line of Indjic and his people and the Main Staff and that they exchanged information and that then that was conveyed to me, that I accept was possible. But right now when you ask me what this is exactly about, I could not remember. Well, that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your corps also received information about civilian casualties in Bosnian-held Sarajevo caused by shelling and sniping of SRK forces from line crossers as well. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't quite understand this thing about crossing lines. I don't quite understand what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This last bit, I don't quite understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At transcript page 37196, you said 15 to 20 persons a day were coming from Bosnian-controlled parts of Sarajevo to SRK-controlled territory. Okay? So can you confirm that your corps also received information about civilian casualties from those people?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it didn't happen every day that 15 people crossed the line entering the territory of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I don't remember. Perhaps the figure is a bit too big. Perhaps it happened only a few times, only in 1993, as far as I can remember. There were other situations when a smaller number of people crossed over. Now, whether we received such reports from them, we did receive reports especially regarding the casualties among the Serb civilians in Sarajevo, in the area of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. They were in different camps there --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and now whether -- well, you just want me to say whether we had committed some crime. I don't know what it is that you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: From line crossers did you receive -- did your corps receive information that civilian casualties were being caused in Bosnian-held Sarajevo by shelling and sniping from SRK forces?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember such information. I said what the information I received was, the information that got to me. I did not question these persons who crossed the lines, and there is a service that deals with that. These are the security and intelligence people, and then they then report to me. They're the ones who interview them and that's how they receive information. I received information primarily about what I already spoke of. Now, whether there was information on other losses when infantry fire was opened and mortar fire and other artillery, I cannot remember right now. But I said during the examination-in-chief that when military targets were engaged, we counted on the possibility of collateral loss of civilian lives. So it is possible that when engaging a military target there could have been civilian casualties, but I do not remember that it is these persons who crossed the lines that provided such information to me. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your indulgence for a moment. Now, you said -- you said to me that -- and in your testimony in chief that you were responsive to each and every one of the protests that you received so long as they were in writing, in a particular format, and contained specific information. And you told me at transcript page 37650 that in Additional Protocol 1 it's defined what a protest is and what it needs to contain. So what I'd like to know is who specifically did you tell in UNPROFOR about this format that you needed to have?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- I mean, all of those who informed me and then when I received protests I would respond, and later on when I had conversations. I said what would be good, and I underlined that several times. I said what this kind of protest should contain and that it should come after a warning, if you will, in terms of what had happened in a particular area. We have to understand -- I mean, we have to go into the situation of urban warfare involving, say, half a million people. Although there are civilians, but they are exposed to this war activity. So on the one hand we have 10.000, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in relation to Sarajevo itself, and the 1st Corps of the Army of BH inside, we've already said they had even up to 45.000 according to some estimates. Now, when such a force is engaged in warfare, when there is activity every day, manoeuvres, and so on, now, all the things that happen and what I should receive in order to be able to take specific measures in my unit, in my corps so that I could say, all right, now I can on the basis of that take measures, say, in the 2nd Brigade or the 1st Brigade or the Igman Brigade, or any brigade. I've already explained what the problems are when we get this protest in principle. As for these specific protests, we saw what my answers were. There's no secret there. We discussed this during the examination-in-chief, and we saw what my response was. There's no secret there. However, would I like to underline once again in this situation when something happened -- now, if we are to interpret this as sniping activity or sniping incidents, as you say, I say that this is an incident due to infantry fire or shelling and then I say due to mortar fire and, all right, other artillery fire. Now what are all the things that I should be receiving in order to be sure that I'm taking the right kind of measures and see what I can focus on, because now to examine three or four brigades, you know, that's a process. You cannot go into all of that. Although I wanted to make the brigade aware of each and every protest I received in writing or verbally. I sent all of that down to the command so that they could be checked. I've already said that during the examination-in-chief too. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember the question I asked you, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, put it again if I haven't answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was: Who specifically did you tell in UNPROFOR about this format that you needed to have your information in? Who specifically? Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of those who talked to me, I told all of them what was necessary in order for me to work more efficiently in that area, because let's look at it this way: It's not that simple. Protest, a shell was fired somewhere, and now you do whatever. I've already told you about some incidents that occurred, that we were never allowed to go there with our forces, except in this one particular case, with our own representatives to go to the actual scene so that we could see where the azimuth was and the line of descent and so on, to check whether this was true or not. So we had to trust them. We had to believe all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 21, in line 15, the General said: "That's a process. That is impossible. It is impossible to examine that," and that was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, these people who you told this to, where in protocol 1 did you point them to? I want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the LiveNote doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, on the personal computer it seems to have stopped, but in the public one it's continuing. Shall we continue? So shall we continue, and in the meantime we can see whether it can be fixed, otherwise we'll take a break. Let's continue for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, could you tell us where in protocol 1 you pointed these people to?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I'm not a lawyer. I'm a soldier. I have read, I have studied those conventions, and protocols 1 and 2. As far as I can remember, I didn't understand who protected us, under whose protections should we have implemented everything that was required by conventions that were issued in 1949? I pointed Article 90 to them, if you want to be very specific. I believe -- and we're talking about protocol 1, Article 9 [as interpreted], protocol 1. A reference is made to commissions -- let me explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, what we're doing is we're talking about your reference at transcript page 37650 to how in international regulations, and I'll quote you: "It is defined what a protest is and what it needs to contain. It is defined in protocol 1 what a report should contain, if it is supposed to contain a schematic for me to see, and based on that schematic I would know from which the shell had come." So I want to know where in protocol 1 you pointed them to for that. Where does it say that in protocol 1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer -- before you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, just a second. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have two points to make on the transcript. I didn't hear in Serbian that General Galic talked about Article 9, but he will tell us. And the second point is that I really have this feeling that he was answering the question. He was asked where in the text. He doesn't have a text, and he doesn't have a document in front of him, and I don't think that this is a process which is acceptable in courtesy terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I respectfully disagree, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I am of the opinion that Mr. Galic is following the question. Yes, please continue, Mr. Galic. If you -- at any moment you do not understand the question, please let us know, and ask Ms. Edgerton to repeat her question at any time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. The question was about the conventions. There's no word "protest" either in the convention or in protocol 1. Let's be very precise about that. Let's say what a protest is and what its form is. However, I pointed Article 90 to them. I don't know under which number, whether it was 5, 6, or 7. I don't know off my head where reference is made to the work of commissions which are in charge of establishing a grave violations of the convention provisions. I told them that if an incident happened, then it was a violation of those convention. At the end of the day we were all part of a learning process during that war, myself as well as UNPROFOR. I had never been in a war before. I knew some of the theory. As for what I needed to know, what measures I had to take, I could only see when I encountered problems during the war. Let us see what is that commission has to establish and how that work of that commission is defined, how the commission is formed, and what reports. You asked me. I'm answering.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But -- just a moment, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin is on his feet again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see you. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to be on my feet again, and I'm listening to the Serbian, and I don't feel -- I don't think that General Galic said a while ago that if an incident occurred, then this was in violation of these conventions. This is not what General Galic said. He didn't say that every time an incident occurred that this was a violation of the convention. He said something else. I don't wish to say it. I don't wish to repeat what he said, but he did not say that, and that is what is on the transcript. If you asked me what he has said, I will gladly tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, do you confirm what Mr. Piletta-Zanin has said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a big problem, I am saying a lot. Whether I said that, whether I worded that in that way or not, it's very difficult for me to say because I can't see the transcript. I don't know how my words were translated. And now for me to say whether that was indeed said in that way or not, it's a big problem. Please appreciate that. I'm very honest. I'm honest to the very end. So I don't think that it is any problem working with me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Honest." I would translate it rather "sincere" or "frank" than "honest." Because General Galic said "iskren" not "castan."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if there's much difference, but thank you. I'll leave it to you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I may make a suggestion, Your Honour, with respect to Mr. Piletta-Zanin's interventions on the transcript. All of us in the courtroom, when we feel there is something that warrants review, have at the end of the day to fill out a form which avoids us interrupting the proceedings, and that form is then submitted to the appropriate services. And I would think that in the spirit of helpfulness, this is why Mr. Piletta-Zanin takes his feet, but it would be equally helpful if he filled out the form like the rest of us do at the end of the day. Dr. Karadzic, defending himself, of course, we always accept his interventions because they're well placed and it's difficult for him to do the same, but I wonder if -- if these are issues that Mr. Piletta-Zanin is going to continually take to his feet over, perhaps it would be more efficient that he did this either at the end of the session or on paper like the rest of us do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate his endeavour if it is related to something that is important for all the parties and the Chamber, but otherwise he must have taken your point. Let us continue. Shall we leave it at that? Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And because of these interventions I don't actually have a way to go back in the transcript, Your Honour, to see where we left off. If you can give me a moment, please. Because of the interventions and the fact that the LiveNote doesn't work on personal computers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: If I may suggest to disconnect and reconnect, and you'll get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton must appreciate your advice. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, General, as we continue, I want to say while I appreciate you feel you have information that you want to give to the Chamber, the more you could focus on answering my questions, the less time you'll have to spend listening to me. So we'll continue. General, you keep referring to these commissions and how important you feel their work might be, but if you look at the UNMOs' jobs, it was their job, among other things, that if they found an attack against civilians was happening, it was their job to get it to stop, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tasks of UN representatives or UNMOs or other representatives of the United Nations, commanders, all those who visited me, I knew more or less what tasks they had, because when they visited me, they mostly sought solutions to the problems that bothered them and less for those that bothered me, i.e., the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. As for UNMOs, we saw a schematic, if we all remember that schematic, about the deployment of UNMOs in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps of BiH Army --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, General --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer. I will answer. I will answer. You will not understand me if you don't allow me to answer completely. If we had four observation points in that large area, I said eight, I thought that there were more than there actually were, so I didn't know whether there were four or eight, but I saw in the schematic that there were four. In such a large city with 400.000 people living there in the Muslim part of Sarajevo, i.e., in the part of Sarajevo under the control of the BiH Army, there were four men, i.e., four observation posts. How could they cover everything? How could they see anything between the high-rise buildings, other facilities, and other obstacles --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, this has nothing to do with the question I asked you. My question was: Among the jobs they had -- among the jobs they had, if the UNMOs saw an attack against civilians was happening, it was their job to get it to stop. Are you disputing that?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, you're a lawyer, I'm a soldier, and we look at things differently. I agree with you. Military observers were duty-bound to say what was happening if they saw what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They needed to report what they saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So is there any sense --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure witness has answered the question. Witness answered that it is their job to say what was happening, but the question was whether it is the UNMOs' obligation to stop what they are observing if civilians were being attacked. What is your answer, Mr. Galic, about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is correct, but I was interrupted while I was answering the question. I wanted to be put in a situation where I would be able to answer properly. In the examination-in-chief, I answered along these lines: That at any time, at any moment, whether an attack was legitimate or not, if we received information that there were civilian casualties during such an attack, that the attack would be called off immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reading your question again. You said "Get it to stop." Yes, please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To get the shelling to stop -- to get shelling to stop, UNMOs had to act urgently; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In war, all situations are urgent, madam, and especially if there are civilian casualties. I agree that this would be one of the most urgent tasks that had to be seen to, and if such a report was received, it was probably received by Indjic's office. It didn't reach me. Indjic testified here. He testified in my case as well. You have said he testified in this case as well, and he told you what reactions were and how he followed up on the warnings and protests that he received from UNMOs, i.e., UNPROFOR representatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So given the urgency of the situation when there's an ongoing shelling attack against civilians, General, what sense is there in asking for written information and -- about the incident and a schematic for you to work with? Because that would have made -- insisting on that would have made it impossible for the UNMOs to do their jobs, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have been mixing apples and oranges here. If something is urgent and if there is a telephone call asking for a resolution, we also used telephone. Indjic used his telephone. If he can't deal with the situation on his own, he calls either me or somebody in charge of the situation that needed to be looked at, and then all the brigades in the zone are called if the direction of fire is known, and they are warned to abort any attacks, whether it is a fire that was being opened or an infantry attack. So we didn't wait for schematics to arrive. However, when you tried me here, you brought schematics without which you could not try me. So if I were put in a position to try somebody or to be a judge of somebody, I had to have schematics and drawings. How else would I have been able to do my job properly?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, General, when you were given more details, what you needed, you still didn't respond to UN protests, did you? When you got the written letter, when you got the time, when you got the date, you were still unresponsive. Isn't that actually the case?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What have I been telling you for five days here during the examination-in-chief, for example? We saw the instances when I responded, how I responded. Mr. Karadzic was examining me for five days, and I answered his questions. So how can you now say that I did not respond to such protests? I really don't seem to be able to understand things here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at another document. It's P1061. It's a protest letter to you from the Sector Sarajevo commander on the 21st of February, 1993, and it's about shelling attacks on UNPROFOR. And it sets out the date. It indicates in the letter that you well knew where the UN positions that were endangered and damaged were located. It sets out the time, and it calls for an investigation calling the attacks intolerable. Even when you got these kind of details and this kind of specific information, General, in fact you were singularly unresponsive, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where will I find that? Where does it say that I didn't do anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you answer this protest then, General? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the letters. Can the letter be zoomed in a little, because I can't read. It's really difficult to remember what anybody wrote 20 years ago. I might remember some details, but not all of them. I don't know now --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, General, over the course of your tour, did you ever answer any protest with anything other than a denial?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am going back to my previous answer. I don't know what to say. Your question is repetitive. I can only repeat what I already said, what I did based on oral and written protests. And now you're telling me that I only denied protests. This is not correct. If I received protests, and this is about a vehicle that was shot at, I don't know where that happened. However, there were protests about shelling going on in the vicinity of command posts of UNPROFOR, but before that, we warned them that from that area Muslim forces had been opening fire on us. I can't remember whether anybody responded or not to that mortar fire by BiH Army. I don't know whether any of the UNPROFOR command posts were affected by that. I can't remember. If we can find it somewhere, please point it to me. After that, I warned UNPROFOR. I protested myself. In the examination-in-chief, we read documents where we warned the Muslim side not to take positions, not to provoke our side from the vicinity of command posts or the deployment of UNPROFOR forces. So they were warned and they did not take measures. And if that was the case, who would be to blame if fire continued to be opened from those areas, which was the case. So I did take measures. I warned them to move their forces from their area of deployment. I remember that the same thing happened when they moved their observation post to Zuc. They had --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you answer my question? My question was: Did you ever answer any protest with anything other than a denial? Did you ever answer any protest admitting responsibility?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, my answer was not a denial. I first checked, and then whatever reports I received from my subordinate units I referred those reports further. I checked in the subordinated commands. I told you how they reported to me, what answers I received. They would tell me that it was their response to fire or that they didn't open fire. If they responded to fire, it was a legitimate action. There was nothing to investigate. I did not receive any more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the second question. Was there any incident in which you answered admitting the SRK's responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I could not admit anything because I did not have enough information so as to be able to admit to such an incident. I didn't have enough information. This is what I've been repeating. How can I admit something that was just said to me? Later on, when they provided me with more information or reports, I could have perhaps admit things, but if there's just a reference to something, when I checked those things with my units, I could only create my indicia suspecting that something was wrong -- that something was wrong. Let me tell you, there were situations when I myself says that those reports that were received on excessive use of fire and firing equipment, that those reports were rather correct, and sometimes fire was excessive. Now, whether the fire is proportionate or not, it's a different issue. It's up to the commander how to decide on the proportionality of fire. It doesn't say anywhere. It depended on the military goal that one needed to be achieved. If the goal was to neutralise a target, I can't tell you what happened. Those who ordered fire, they also assessed what their objective was. I don't remember that I issued an order to a corps commander to open fire. It was in the hands of lower ranked commands. However, if you will allow me, I will continue. Perhaps things will become more clear to you. Within the framework of those indicia, I felt that there were actions that should have been more proportionate, and based on those indicia, I removed -- or, rather, I did not remove because I didn't have the right to do that, I proposed that a brigade commander, a battalion commander be removed from their positions. The first commander, the brigade commander lacked discipline and he used equipment and assets that were excessive, and as for the second commander, I don't know whether I was right. I'm still not sure that I was right when I thought that she -- he should be removed from his position. That was my answer, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Back to you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to follow up on what you've just told to His Honour Judge Kwon, can you tell us who the brigade commander -- actually, let me read you back your answer. You said: "I proposed that a brigade commander, a battalion commander, be removed from their positions. The first commander, the brigade commander, lacked discipline, and he used equipment and assets that were excessive, and as for the second commander, I don't know whether I was right." Can you tell us who those two people are?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if this is what the transcript says, but these are not my words, but the essence is there, I would say, and that's the most important thing. The essence is there. This means that I accepted suggestions, but I did not have enough proof to take somebody to court-martial or things like that, but there were indicia, and based on those indicia the first commander was the commander of the Igman Brigade, Dunjic, he lacked discipline. He was rather wilful. He used excessive force according to my estimates and my indicia. I can't say whether that was indeed true or not, because one would have to go to the area to see what the effects were. I couldn't go to the Muslim side either with my commission or my forces. I could not rely on UNPROFOR to allow me to do that. And the second commander was the battalion commander in Nedzarici and his name was Grkovic. I understood him. When we explained the positions in Nedzarici, when we explained his position, there were four brigades there and during that time or before that he saw what had happened in Pofalici when Pofalici fell. He did not have a reserve position, a reserve homeland. He did not have anything reserved. He had to defend and protect Nedzarici. So any movement by such large forces that he expected would happen demanded that he engaged as many people as possible in order to thwart those attacks, and that's why he always asked from the brigade commanders and his neighbours and he also sought approval from the corps command to perhaps engage artillery and heavy artillery assets, possibly in a more unproportionate way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You mean Radivoje Grkovic?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So did you remove him or not? Because it's not clear from your answer.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's clear, but I said that I proposed that. I had no right to remove anyone. That was not my authority. I could only make the proposal for someone to be removed from office, and then the organs of the corps command would propose it further, and then it would be approved at the level of the Main Staff via the ministry which is in charge of appointing officers up to the rank of colonel. And they were the ones who were able to remove him from office and to decide whether he would remain in a similar or other position, what measures would be taken, disciplinary or others.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, that's clear now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see it's 10.33, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but your answer is that you proposed to remove him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that was my -- I had no authority to remove him. As the commander of corps, I could not remove a brigade commander. The brigade commanders were appointed by the Ministry of Defence, and the generals were appointed by the Superior Command -- or, rather, the president. So I could not order something that I did not have the authority to appoint such a person. I could only propose certain measures with an explanation or a statement of reasons that he be removed, appointed to a different position, or that disciplinary measures be taken against him. That was my authority. I couldn't remove him and say, Well, from this day on you're no longer a commander. I just did not have such authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. To whom and how did you make that proposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those proposals were submitted to the Main Staff, the Main Staff. All our communications, proposals, opinions, were sent via the Main Staff, and then they would regulate the relations with the Ministry of Defence whether such an officer would remain in position or would be removed, who would replace him, because up there in the Igman Brigade, a number of commanders were changed not for this reason but for some other reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect to Mr. Grkovic, is your evidence that you submitted a recommendation to the Main Staff for measures to be taken against him?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be more precise here, and to give a more simple answer, he was a battalion commander. His immediate superior was the commander of the brigade, Radojcic, it was at the time. It was his duty to submit such a proposal or recommendation. He would submit such a proposal through the corps command. That would then be sent to the Main Staff, and the Main Staff and the Ministry of Defence would regulate between themselves the appointments of officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did that happen, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it did. He was removed from office, from that position. He was from Montenegro, and simply I believe that he left for Montenegro. Considering the situation he was in, I would say that I was quite tolerant towards him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at six past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It might be too quick given the stage, but can I ask you how much do you expect your cross to last in light of the fact that we are sitting only for three days this week?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I am confident I'll be able to give Your Honours an accurate estimate at the end of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, I'd like to come back to something you said in answering one of my questions this morning. At the transcript at page 32, you mentioned receiving protests of shelling going on in the vicinity of the UN command post, and you said then also that you warned the UN that Muslims had been opening fire from that area and asked who was to be blamed if fire was opened from those areas, and then you went on to talk about proportionality. And I recall during your examination-in-chief you said, actually, at transcript page 37571, that: "Neither the equipment nor the command posts or the positions of the UN were ever targeted by us." That seems to contrast with your testimony today, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Madam Prosecutor, that is your view, but I think that it's not contrary at all. My forces never targeted the disposition, let me call it that way, or the command posts of the United Nations as far as I know. We have said today that there were examples like this one when some areas of the airport were targeted, but later on it was established that some other side did it, the 1st Corps of the BH Army. And as for the command posts, they opened fire at mortars -- or, rather, the disposition of firing corps -- firing forces of the 1st Corps of the BH Army rather than the observation posts of UNPROFOR or the observers. And I said after that whether there could have been some consequences for the command post of the military observers or the command post of UNPROFOR. I don't remember that there was anything special. I know that in conversation with Razek, General Razek he promised that he would lodge a protest with the Muslims for such fire, but that was repeated again from those sectors where the disposition of the command post of UNPROFOR were. This is why I said so. We did not target UNPROFOR command posts. That was not the target of any attack or fire. It was not the target.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember, General, Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler who testified in the trial against you in 2002? An UNMO from New Zealand.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember all the military observers. He was not a leader of the military observers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the contents of his testimony, so if you could please refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I'll actually show you a document. It's 65 ter number 14217. It's a letter to you, and it's dated 13 February 1993 from Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler. It was Exhibit P798 from your trial, and this is, as you see from the very first paragraph, the second of two letters he wrote to you in response to what he says is the repeated deliberate shelling by your forces of his OP, of his observation post. And he also notes that he verbally protested to your Chief of Staff at the time. And despite a letter of complaint to you on the 30th of January, and that's at the bottom of paragraph 1, and the visit where Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler was reassured that your corps knew the locations of all observation posts, his post Papa 5 was shelled again on the 13th of February. And in your trial at transcript page 8926, he spoke of the shelling on the 13th, saying it was 60 rounds of 122-millimetre artillery which landed near the observation posts some 2 to 3 metres away from the building. So it seems as though your assertion that you -- your forces never targeted UN dispositions or command posts is incorrect, doesn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You always try to assert that what I say is incorrect. You could not take into account other circumstances, what I said and what the context was, what the conditions were. Whether it's true or not, I will explain it to you now. I don't know where exactly this OP was located, Papa 5. If we had four, then Papa 5 was on the Muslim side. Whether it was in the sector of -- I cannot find it immediately, in which sector it was located, the particular observation post. If you told me that, I could perhaps give you a more detailed answer to your question, because I certainly guarantee that my forces never targeted observation posts or command posts of the military observers, but what did happen sometimes was that they would change their positions. They would be here one day and then on the next day perhaps we did not have sufficient information that they had changed their positions, and the Muslims, that is to say, the 1st Corps of the BH Army, fired from there. Then we would respond target that area and then it would turn out that it was close to an observation point. So you can see from this that it was not directly targeted even if it was too close. But 3 metres is 3 metres. It is too close but still. And I don't know what duty this gentleman, Mr. Cutler was discharging. Was he a military observer or was he the chief of the military observers on the Muslim side, or what was he? What was his duty?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you can just scroll down to the bottom of the page, you can see that he was the senior military observer. Now --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he -- he was rather a military observer but on the Muslim side. That's -- if such an incident occurred, it's only possible that they change their position and that we did not know about that. As I said, that is possible, but I wouldn't know. I have told you about the situation in Zuc. That was a situation I do remember. When they were assigned -- I wanted to tell you about that, but then you interrupted me, if you remember. They had changed the location of their observation post and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I interrupted you --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and they located it next to the cannons and -- well, once again you're interrupting me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- because I didn't ask you anything about Zuc. Because you weren't answering my question. So --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you haven't told me where this observation post was. Where is Papa 5, in which sector? I don't remember Papa, Lima 11, 12, 15, and all these designations. After 20 years I'm to remember where each position was. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Why would that make a difference, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that it would greatly change things because I would know how to answer you. Right now I don't know how to answer you. You want me to tell you what I know. I'm telling you what I know, but I cannot tell you about things that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're denying that this, in fact, took place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You didn't understand me correctly, madam. I'm telling you that I -- I say what I know. I would not like to make any speculations here, because you agree with me and I see that you requested that no speculations should be made. Whether it was so or not, and if I have the arguments with which to explain that. I don't have sufficient arguments based on which I could explain this document. It's not my document. It's a document from one Cutler. I have no idea who or what he was. You say he was at my trial but you know how many of these people were in my trial, all these UNPROFOR members and everyone else. And I'm supposed to remember whether he said something or not in 2002 when my trial was still ongoing. I can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in answering one of my questions you insisted that the -- this OP wasn't directly targeted but, in fact, perhaps we could look at another document, 65 ter number 14208. It's another letter of protest to you from Cutler, dated 14 February 1993. Now, the very first paragraph, the last line says Papa 5 was intentionally shelled actually four times, the 30th of January, the 13th of February in the morning, the 13th of February at noon, and on the 14th of February, wounding, as you see at the top of the second paragraph, an UNMO. And Cutler asserts on the basis of the events that transpired that the shooting came from positions under control of your corps and was intentional. It was direct targeting, General. So again this seems to -- the observations of Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler directly contradict your assertion about targeting UNPROFOR, don't they?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your assertion. You have some paper here that I'm looking at now addressed to me, as far as I can see, up on top. It's interesting that all of this is written by one and the same person, Cutler, and not in some other location. So this can also be somewhat indicative. But I'm sorry if a military observer was hit regardless of the side from which the shell came, whether from the side of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps or from the side of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. I cannot answer anything to this question of his, because I don't remember that this was present like this in my area. This was the month of February 1993. All of these events have to do with that month. That means that some combat was ongoing there. Something was happening in the sector where this Papa 5 observation point was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, in fact, in your trial, in response to a concern that there might have been outgoing fire nearby, Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler specifically testified at transcript pages 8925 and 8926 that he investigated this assertion and found no evidence to confirm it, General. So it appears, again contrary to what you say, that there was no outgoing fire in the area, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, as I said, I did not testify in my trial. I requested that, but it was not allowed. I have come to testify in this trial and in this case in order to try to represent the truth more or less about what was happening in Sarajevo and how, and you have been asserting throughout that I am trying to conceal something or that I'm not telling the truth, which in practical terms I don't like because that's not true. If I don't know what some paper contains 20 years later, it's not a matter of me not telling the truth, but I simply don't remember. That is why I always ask to be told what is the general context of a situation so that I can try to refresh my memory, because you will allow that a lot of time has passed and many things did happen in two years. To remember now what was going on in a specific location on a specific day, well, I'm telling you anything I can during my testimony, and after all, I'm just a witness here. So I will answer to all the questions when I'm able to and when I remember. What I don't know, I don't know, or I don't remember or I didn't see. I know that there were some problems with this Papa, but whether things developed exactly as stated here, I don't know. I don't remember. It's possible. But my order was that it was not allowed to target or fire against UN personnel commands, observation posts, or anything, and I was quite resolute. I requested to have co-operation with them and not to kill them, and I'm really sorry to read here that this man from the observation point was wounded. Whether the shell had come from our side or from which side, this is something I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've just said that you know that there were some problems with this Papa, although you said a few minutes before that you didn't know the location at which it was, and I would like to know what the problems were that you remember.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I remember that this Papa and the position of this observation post was not good because it was not visible enough from the position of our forces. That's what I do remember. Another thing. I remember that they were too close to the disposition of the Muslim forces. And thirdly, I remember that after that they may have changed their position. So this is more or less what I do remember. But for me to remember all of this in detail, and how can I claim whether it's true or not? All right. This is a report that was drawn up, but we have no investigation here. We cannot establish whether it was the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps or some other forces that were shelling, and without any work of commissions and all of that to claim or assert that the shells had come from the side of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, all right, it's information that such an incident happened and that we should prevent them, but to be able to take disciplinary measures or to prosecute someone before such an incident is investigated, that was something that I couldn't do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you said here -- you've said just now that you couldn't establish whether it was the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps or some other forces that were shelling without any work of commissions. In fact, General, your Chief of Staff was specifically confronted, specifically protested, with the shelling of this observation post. He specifically told Cutler, and that's in 65 ter 14217, the first document that we saw, that you knew where the observation posts were. So why do you need a commission in the face of a protest like you've just seen from Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I don't understand you. Do you understand me? If there was a protest, I don't remember whether I received it or not. Where I was, I have no idea. But if there was a protest that was lodged, and if the Chief of Staff knew where this Papa 5 was, where, but it doesn't necessarily mean that it was visible. Another thing, how can we accept that it is such on the face of it just to believe it? Well, a shell fell there and it was fired by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. This is why a report would be necessary, whether the report of a commission or somebody else, an on-site investigation should be conducted, and the azimuth and the direction would be established and it could be said, well, it came from such and such a position on the basis of the azimuth and so on. I cannot now -- this is why say I cannot answer such questions, whether it was a shell or something else that was fired from the positions of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps or from the positions of the 1st Corps of the BH Army, because there are all kinds of military observers. Some of them liked Serbs, others didn't. Some were good, others were not. Some were reliable, others were not. Some wanted to gain popularity for themselves in various ways. I don't know.
