It was a war going on. And to trust something, to believe something, to believe the military observers, well, I believed them as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you needed a report of a commission, if you needed an on-site investigation, if you needed the azimuth, if you needed the direction, why didn't you or any member of your staff tell that to Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked that and I already told you about that. With regard to all these incidents, this is one of the incidents, too, but in terms of the United Nations, I cautioned you about that when the commission went to the airport and investigated matters, although they said it was the Serb side that had fired the shells, it turned out that it was the Muslim side that had fired them. That is why it is important to have a site investigation. Any crime, I mean even today, you have to go to the scene, and you have to reach certain parameters in order to convict a person or suggest that somebody else be convicted with regard to that kind of problem, let alone in a war. That is why it is necessary to have that part of the documents that we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, with respect, you didn't answer my question. Do you want me to repeat it to you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that I did answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you needed -- my question was: If you needed a commission report or an on-site investigation or the azimuth or the direction of fire, why didn't you or anybody in your staff tell that to Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, perhaps the transcript did not reflect what I had said. If necessary, I'll repeat it yet again. I said that I asked for that with regard to each and every incident that I was told about, protests, whatever, to submit this kind of information. So with regard to this incident, that should have been asked for. Now, whether it had been asked for or had not, I cannot say right now, but this was well known. As a matter of fact, all these commissions work under the supervision and control of UNPROFOR. So UNPROFOR and the military observers, they lead these mixed commissions. Just like in the mixed commission the leader is, I don't know, from the UNPROFOR command for BH. For Sector Sarajevo, the leader of the commission is such and such a person from Sector Sarajevo. It's not the representative of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps or the representative of the 1st Corps of the BH Army that is the leader of the commission, so they should have asked for it themselves. And I said during the examination-in-chief if we hadn't done something properly, in accordance with conventions and so on and so forth, they should have taught us. They should have taught us how we should do things and what we should do. As for this commission, this commission had to --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, I'll try this one more time and then we'll move on, but nobody answered Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler. That's the evidence we have got in front of us. If he needed to give you something more for you to be able to do something, why didn't you tell him? Instead, you just didn't answer. Nobody in your staff answered.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say. You said yourself that it was the Chief of Staff who talked to them so that means I wasn't there, and I don't really know this entire process, what happened. Now for me to claim whether this or that thing was given -- I mean, I'm just giving you the general principles and orders that I had issued and that everyone was supposed to abide by. Now, whether it was said or not said, I cannot say, but probably this Cutler, if he came that many times bringing these protests, he himself, and it is not his duty to bring protests to the corps command because he is the observer for the Muslim side primarily, not for the Serb side, if that's it. So if he's a senior observer, then it's only in the area of where it is the area of one corps or the other corps, but then also there is the chief observer who was supposed to co-operate with both sides, if that's the way it is. Perhaps he was the chief observer then. Really I cannot say, because they changed then. Was it Valentin then or not? Whether he got in instead of Valentin I --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have these two documents, please, 65 ter 14217 and 14208 as Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P6298 and Exhibit P6299 respectively.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to talk about some of the incidents that Dr. Karadzic asked you about during your examination-in-chief, but not for a great deal of time, and we will start by talking about some of the sniping incidents. Now, with respect to what we call sniping incident F6, that's an incident that took place on the 6th of January, 1994, in the context of a discussion about this incident where a woman was shot while riding a bicycle across the Nikola Demonja Street, the bridge there in Dobrinja. You said you "wanted to celebrate holidays peacefully, not only Sarajevo but everywhere else. We wanted peace for Muslims as well as for ourselves," and that's at transcript page 37521. And you also referred to a document Dr. Karadzic showed you, D3452. And we could have a look at that so the General could refresh his memory. It's your daily combat report to the Main Staff of the same date. And looking at this document, you told Dr. Karadzic that you didn't see reference to any activities across that bridge, and that's at 37522. And after having a quick look at that document, I'd like to turn to another one, P -- just tell me when you've had a look at it, General, and we can move on. Are we all right to move on, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not that much of a genius. Thank you very much, but, yes, then we can move on to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could have a look at P2293. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask to zoom in because I don't really see any of this. So regardless of whether I have the document in front of me or not in this form, it doesn't matter. Now, this is better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now are we moving to the next document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If the General's -- if the General's okay with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- is an UNMO Zagreb weekly summary for the period of 31 December 1993 to 6 January 1994 which discusses the scale of shelling activity during this holiday time, and unfortunately it's only in English, General, so I'll read it to you. If we could go to e-court page 3 of the English. Under heading B, which is Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then sub-1, Sarajevo, and then sub a and b, it reports Sarajevo as being unstable throughout the reporting period, and at b says there was BSA, Bosnian Serb Army, shelling of the northern and western areas of the city, along with the city centre all week long. Most frequent Bosnian Serb Army targets were Stup with coordinates, Zuc with coordinates, Alipasino Most with coordinates, Smiljevici and Rajlovac, also with coordinates. It then says the level of Bosnian Serb Army shelling rose from 123 outgoing rounds at the beginning of the week to 1.613 outgoing on the 4th of January, 1.344 outgoing on the 5th of January, and 815 impacts on the 6th of January, 1994. So regardless, General, of your express desire in your evidence in chief to celebrate the holidays peacefully, it doesn't seem that that's the case at all, and what your soldiers were doing at the time is that they were engaged in heavy shelling, as well as the sniping of civilians as occurred in this incident F6. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not the case. Now, why is that not the case? All of this shelling is outside Dobrinja. You see, it has nothing to do with Dobrinja, Zuc, et cetera. It's far away from Dobrinja and all the areas where there was fighting and so on that they reported on. All right, now whether it's that way and how they counted it, whose, what, but these areas are not related to Dobrinja where this incident where we're speaking about happened, this sniping incident as you call it, or one related to infantry fire in the area of Dobrinja. If I remember directly what it was that you asked me about. So I would not -- that is why I would say that that is not linked to that area, but I do agree that if there were such provocations and if one had to respond and if one could not peacefully celebrate any holiday, that was possible, it wouldn't have been the first time. After all, this characteristic in relation to provocations, I mean of the BH Army, that was present throughout the war. I spoke about the names of some operations, what we called them, operation step-by-step to intervention, that is to say, to engage as many forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as possible and to portray that as some kind of terror rather than targeting military targets. That is why linking all of this to what happened in Dobrinja, sorry, I don't really see any link. If you see one, do tell me. Perhaps I didn't listen carefully enough, but I did listen carefully and I didn't find anything. So that claim, that is correct, that there was intensified artillery fire there and that can be seen from these reports now. Whether it was that way or not, I mean I have to believe it. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- repeat once again, they have no reason to lie.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- to be fair, I'm going to read you subparagraph c of this report. It says that Bosnian shelling --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- was mainly confined to areas of Lukavica, Grbavica, and the Bosnian Serb Army side of the confrontation line in the Vogosca area. So none of the areas referred to in the first paragraph. And says the level of Bosnian shelling fluctuated between 10 and 50 rounds throughout the week.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. I did take a look at this paragraph C. You know where Grbavica is. It's down there. Hrasno, Hrasno Brdo, Mojmilo, separates it from Dobrinja, so this really has nothing to do with Dobrinja, this Grbavica. Now let us move on. Vogosca, you know where Vogosca is. That is on the completely opposite side of the front in relation to Dobrinja. So that's it. All right. If that's what happened. But again we cannot link this to Dobrinja, what happened, I mean, when this incident occurred, please, if that is what matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, General, how does small levels of outgoing Bosnian shelling in Lukavica, Grbavica, and the Serbian side of the confrontation lines in Vogosca justify response to completely unrelated areas, Stup, Zuc, Alipasino Most, Smiljevici and Rajlovac, and the level of 1.613 rounds and almost the same amount, 1.344, as this document says, on the 4th and 5th of January?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I kindly ask that we be given an explanation on the basis of what it says that this is unrelated, unrelated locations? Where is it written that they did not fire at Serb positions from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was supposed to be my question too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll leave it to you Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I can change to word to "other areas." Should I rephrase the question for you, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever you prefer. I can answer, no problem. It's better to rephrase it so that I understand better, but it's not a problem. Just what Mr. Karadzic asked right now, that's what I wanted to ask. We cannot see whether any fire had come from Zuc. We know that the 1st Corps of the BH Army is in all of these areas where this activity took place. There are no civilian areas there. I mean, now we would have to look specifically to see whether there is anything civilian there. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, so maybe I'll ask the question a different way. Was it your forces' practice to respond in the face of Bosnian attack on other areas of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we recall the examination-in-chief, I said where if I was directed that it was directed to sources of enemy fire, not that there was any kind of revenge taking place in any area. As for the answer I gave to the president, there were situations when there was a disproportionate response and I think that to a considerable extent this is a reply to what you are saying in relation to some problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll leave this for the moment, but we're going to come back to this, General, because I want to talk about another sniping incident, and that's the one on 25 May 1994. We call it F7, and it relates to the targeting of a bus in Dobrinja. And in discussion about that incident, you said at transcript page 37522 to 37523: "When I remember that buses were running, people could stroll, that they could work in their gardens, that they could go shopping. What else could we do? What else could we make possible in that area? If public transport was working in the area of Dobrinja, which was under constant fire, as it were, and if people were wounded, the question is who wounded them and whether we could open fire on that bus from our side." Now, when you referred to Dobrinja being under constant fire, you meant constant fire from your forces. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Constant fire because -- well, we had parts of Dobrinja that we held under constant fire of the BH Army and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. So as a matter of fact, even more so. I mean, it's not that I measured this. It is unrealistic to say. But if we recall the number of shells that were fired from both sides, now what is being counted as I don't know which grenade, which shells, but you will see that many shells were fired to the area held by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. That would be the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, this incident is an incident of targeting a bus in Bosnian-held territory in Dobrinja. So I can only assume when you were discussing this incident and in your answer to Dr. Karadzic you were referring to Bosnian-held territory in Dobrinja. I'll remind you what you said: "If public transport was working in the area of Dobrinja which was under constant fire, as it were, and if people were wounded, the question is who wounded them and whether we could open fire on that bus from our side." When you referred to the area of Dobrinja which was under constant fire in your answer to Dr. Karadzic, you were referring to Bosnian-held Dobrinja, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct, because everything I said beforehand is correct. If we look at all of Sarajevo, and if we look at all the incidents that occurred and all the people who were wounded, I am saying that all of this was made possible, for markets to work, for shops to work. I don't want to go into further interpretations, but I'd like to go back to this incident. That is correct too. You know where Dobrinja, and you know how far away this is from the front line, this bus. And you know that this is an area -- well, sort of between high-rise buildings, and where could this fire come from, the fire at this bus? All of this remained unclear. As for this incident during the war, I claim that we had not received a single protest in writing or verbally with regard to any one of these individual sniping incidents that are mentioned in Mr. Karadzic's indictment. That is why I'm saying -- that is why I'm saying everything I know about this bus, all of that dates back to my trial. I did know about it beforehand. I know that there were buses running, and I know that some kind of agreement was sought. It can go, it cannot go, but the position was to enable public transportation. Now, where civilians were going, why they were taking buses, where --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General. General, can we go back to my question --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean if there is a war going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I asked you to confirm that you were referring to Bosnian-held Dobrinja, and you said, "Correct, correct." Now, you meant to say, then -- let me just rephrase that. So according to the answer that you've just given, Bosnian-held Dobrinja was under constant fire and constant fire by your forces. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were constant conflicts. So if there are conflicts, fire is opened. There was no peace there. Let's put it that way. So if there was a cessation in firing, then it was the Muslims who stopped that. And we saw evidence of that during the examination-in-chief here, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, when you gave that answer, when you said, "I remember that buses were running, that people could stroll, that they could work in their gardens, they could go shopping," you were describing the period of cease-fire, weren't you? Because this is May 1994. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you that there were some ten different cease-fires. May 1994, I think there was a cease-fire. I can't say for sure now. But regardless of whether there was a cease-fire or not, it was forbidden to target means of public transportation. Let us be clear on that. Although there is different evidence here --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- in February 1994, a cease-fire agreement was concluded between the warring parties. You were, as you said in your evidence in chief, present with Dr. Karadzic during the course of these negotiations. So are you now saying that that cease-fire was no longer in force by the 25th of May, 1994?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That cease-fire -- you know what? A cease-fire lasts for as long the parties keep it going. If it is not limited by time. If one side violates the cease-fire - that is what is written in conventions too - the other side no longer has the obligation to honour that cease-fire, although we kept saying that we honour the cease-fire. If there is a time limit, then that has to be observed, say, if it was a month. This cease-fire was certainly there on the 18th of February, 1994, and these other activities that were carried out within that framework including the cessation in combat activities. Now, after that, whether there was a halt in May or June, going on for a month, I cannot tell you exactly because I cannot remember all of these different orders that had to do with cease-fires agreements and so on. But I think that then, in June, there was a cease-fire for about a month. I may be wrong on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, we'll definitely come back to this then, General, but for now let's move on to, so we don't get off track from these sniping incidents, the one we call F10 and it took place on the 22nd of July, 1994. And in regard to this incident, a 13-year-old boy was shot in the abdomen while he was window shopping with his mother in Cengic Vila. And you suggested, at least in general, that there may have been Bosnian Army forces deployed in the area of Cengic Vila. You -- and that was at transcript page 37538. You said: "The area in question is Cengic Vila and we can see, if we look at the disposition which forces were deployed there, but there's some information available that there was some unit or troops that were deployed or were moving in that particular area." And that's, by the way, General, that's even though you said on that same page whether there was any firing of that -- "whether there was any firing, what sort of fire or activities, that is something that I couldn't claim at this point in time and this situation." But I want to come back to this observation or suggestion that there may have been Bosnian Army forces deployed in the area of Cengic Vila. General, Brigadier Blagoje Kovacevic, who was, among other things, battalion commander in the -- in your 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, testified here last year, and he was asked whether there were any no-fire zones in Sarajevo, areas not to be targeted, and he said, although it wasn't the only one, there was -- Cengic Vila was a no-fire zone. It never came under fire. Only from Cengic Vila fire was never opened against us. There was no front line in Cengic Vila. It was mostly inhabited by civilians. There were no institutions, no military, and there was no need to open fire on Cengic Vila. So it seems like, General, your suggestion is actually speculative because your contradicted by one of your own commanders. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each commander knew what they knew. Every command level had its information. I don't have to know everything that a battalion commander knew. I was not in a position to know. However, Cengic Vila is in the centre of Sarajevo. It's the very centre of Sarajevo, in practical terms. We insisted on this part, being a museum part, like Bascarsija, for example, it's a museum area, and that it shouldn't be targeted. And I suppose that claim of his originates from there. I don't know what he testified. I didn't hear it. I don't know what he told you. However, this may be my speculation. This is all subsequent knowledge. I'm talking with hindsight. I did not have that information during the war. I didn't know that a lad had been hit. I'm sorry about that young boy. Of course, I'm sorry. It was a 13-year-old child. I didn't know at the time that he was wounded, and I repeat, I'm sorry. I feel sorry for all those who were innocent and who suffered during the war, especially in Sarajevo. Based on my trial, I can tell you that a witness, I don't know which witness, said that an army passed through there, that was said during my trial. This is why I thought that there were troops in that area. I don't know whether they passed through there and whether that boy was with them window shopping. I don't know. But if you look at the deployment of command posts, you will see that there is -- there was a command post somewhere in the vicinity. How does one shell Cengic Vila? The question is where it was shelled from, because it was a problem, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you saying -- so you're now saying there was a command post in Cengic Vila. Did you know that at the time?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I did not know that. I didn't know. Maybe my commanders did, but I personally didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll leave that for now to stay with the theme of sniping. General, in your testimony to Dr. Karadzic, you insisted several times that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had no sniper units - and that was at transcript pages 37191 to 92, 37465, and 37472 - but that's actually not correct, is it, General? The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had sniper units within the Sarajevo -- the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. If you know better what the situation was in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, then fine, you can testify. I'll do something else. But I'm telling you, in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, at the time when I was commander, there were no sniper units. There were snipers, though, and I repeat what I said during the examination-in-chief. We didn't have sniper units. We had snipers. A smaller number of snipers. I told you how they were deployed and used. And now since you're talking about snipers and sniper units, about sniper activity, and you imply that that was the entire infantry weaponry, you can also say, totally outside of the context, that all infantry units are sniper units. I already told you what sniping activity is --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and if this is what you based your knowledge on and if say that all those were sniper units, well, then it's up to you. It's a totally different story.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You keep coming back to that, and I'd like you to listen to my questions instead and answer my questions. We're talking about sniper units, and you've said categorically that at the time that you were commander there were no sniper units. But, General, one of your company commanders, Dragan Maletic, who was in the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade said in his written evidence to this Court that there was a sniper squad in the 2nd Battalion command directly subordinate to the commander. And that's at D2519, page 5, paragraph 31 in B/C/S; page 9 in English. So, General, you're contradicted in your assertion by one of your own company commanders. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I intervene on the transcript? Madam Edgerton said "sniper squad," and General Galic received the interpretation a "sniper company." That may lead to confusion. [In English] Company. It hadn't been said "company" but "squad."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now he must have understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not understand these statements and assertions. To arrive at conclusions based on partial information, if anybody had such units, they should tell us when they were set up, who set them up, under whose command they were. They were not under my command. There were sniping assets. Sniper fire was opened. That's no secret at all. Whether there were units, especially if you say that there were sniper companies, there were no such things. I'm sure of that. I apologise. It is possible those were all reserve officers. I don't know what their position was in the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, but I don't know whether they understood properly what they put on paper, that person, for example, and that's the question that I'm putting to myself. I adhere to my assertion that in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps we did not have sniper units, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By "unit," what do you mean, General? My question is whether you exclude the possibility that there existed a sniper squad in a battalion or company or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will gladly answer your question and believe that we will arrive at the right answer and the right understanding. Snipers usually work in pairs. There's always two people opening sniper fire together. That was the rule, that was part of the tactic for using such assets. I don't know if there were people who made up a unit or a squad of some ten people or so. Maybe they were given a task as a group. I don't know about that. It is possible that things like that happen. If there was a special task, a special mission, if there was an order to be carried out, as I've told you, I was on the sixth level of command and I was not in a position to know how the organisation was adapted to the situation at hand, how they use their assets that they had. In order to be closer to your interpretation, I am saying that things like that are possible but I don't know. And what is a unit? When you say "a unit," it's a group of some 10 people. A platoon has 30 people. A company has a hundred, battalion has 300 to 500 people. These are units and their strengths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: A company has 30 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when Mr. Maletic gave this evidence, General, your assertion is he didn't know what he was talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may be too strong, but I just provided an answer to that. Perhaps, perhaps I am here and I am learning new things. If my subordinates say that they had things like that and I say that they didn't, then I suppose I did not have enough insight into the whole situation. I don't know whether they were set up as a temporary unit. They were not a permanent unit. A permanent unit by establishment in the corps, for example, in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, without any exaggerations, there shouldn't be a sniper unit in such an establishment order.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when Milan Kovacevic, who was deputy commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade, who also served in Grbavica and who gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, stated, and that's at 65 ter number 22117, page 20, when he stated specifically that there were 12 snipers in the 2nd Battalion 's sniper detachment who came to daily battalion meetings, who sometimes got ammunition from the battalion and sometimes from the brigade, your evidence is that the existence of this unit is something that you as commander didn't know about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, those sniper units, i.e., snipers, have to have special ammunition. That's the difference between sniping and opening infantry fire. Those are not bursts of fire but individual shots. They came from the entire brigade. I believe in the battalion there was a dozen such snipers, ten, and it is possible that personally the commander at a certain level in the battalion gave them the task. It is known that even a battalion commander who is in charge of some 10- to 20.000 people issued the tasks to a person with a machine-gun. So it's not surprising that he got a task and conveyed it to somebody else. Kovacevic was through a lot, from Rajlovac to Sarajevo. I don't know what his position was. I don't know. He was probably the commander of the 1st Battalion up there. That was his duty. And he probably didn't say anything wrong. He said that some ten people were gathered with snipers and we were given tasks, and then the battalion commander, the brigade commander, says that all the snipers had to be gathered and used. It's a normal activity during combat operations. For example, you can also gather armoured forces, transporters, APCs, in order to carry out tasks although they do not belong to a certain unit but they will be operational in their zone of operation. They are so-called tactical groups. In this sector it was also possible to gather important assets that could be used or to perhaps counter the sniping activity of the 1st Corps of the BH Army from Marin Dvor, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. On line 2 he said that it was normal, and before that he said that it was allowed and normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now, General, just -- still on the same subject, in your testimony, in your answers to Dr. Karadzic at transcript pages 37466 and 37471, you listed buildings and locations where you said snipers were deployed on the Bosnian side. Now, you also said, at 37466, your snipers were deployed in the high-rises in Grbavica. You mean, I take it, they were deployed in the white skyscrapers on the former Leninova Street when you refer to the high-rises; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your assumption is good. As for the correct and exact places where those snipers were deployed, to be honest, I really don't know. I never toured their positions. And if you put it to me they were there, I don't know. Those were individuals. I did not get around examining their positions, but they changed places. For example, one night they are in one place and the following day they're in a different place. Whether they were on higher floors of the skyscrapers, yes, they were, because they could observe the sniping units of the BH Army that they had and it's a notorious fact. Everybody knows that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you know where the Bosnian snipers were located but you're not sure where your sniper firing positions were located. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I refuse [as interpreted] to say anything to that. This is not what I meant. I know the approximate locations where they were and from which fire was opened on both sides, but to be precise about the buildings or the floors, I don't know. Madam, I was a corps commander. I was not a squad or a company commander, so it is only normal that I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the same problem with the transcript. General Galic never refused to say something like that. He simply said he never expressed that. So he did not deny this. And as you asked me, Mr. President, I'm not intervening. I only intervene when I feel that there is an urgent need to do it. I've refrained from doing that until now, but I'm doing it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you can also confirm, I take that, that your forces had firing positions in the buildings at Metalka 1 and 2; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's in Grbavica; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Metalka 1 and 2 are both in Grbavica. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they opened fire from that sector, our snipers did, because on the other side, fire was opened from the 1st Corps of the BH Army. There were somewhat stronger forces there in order to repel those attacks. I don't know whether they were snipers or whether they had machine-guns. I don't know what they had. In any case, they were at the ready to respond to the fire opened by the 1st Corps and repel their attacks. Those are two very high skyscrapers. As I already told you, I did not live in Sarajevo, so I have problems with the street names, and I apologise, and it was such a long time ago that I can't retain all those things in my head. I've not succeeded in retaining all that in my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll just then leave the question of those details and go on to another area, still talking about sniping. You said at transcript page 37465 that the main task of sharpshooters -- and it relates to how you've just answered a question now, the main task of sharpshooters or sniping activity was to fight and counter enemy sniper activities. So could we understand -- should we understand your evidence as saying that sniping by your forces was military on military?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you also imply sharpshooters in military terms or the way we explained sniping activities? What do you imply in your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can clarify that for the General but it might take a little while, and I just see the time that we're at. I'm in Your Honours' hands. I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, we'll take a break. We'll take a break for 45 minutes and resume at 10 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Court may have noted that a couple of requests for the presence of counsel were filed in the last couple of hours. I simply wanted to note that the Prosecution has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, is the counsel for Mr. Borovcanin, name of the counsel is Cimeric or Cmeric?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's no I, so it's CM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Cmeric, yes. So the request for the presence of counsel in court during the testimony for Mr. Martic and Borovcanin, i.e., the presence of attorney Mr. Bourgon and Ms. Cmeric, are hereby granted. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, we left off with my question to you as to whether we should understand your evidence as saying sniping by your forces was military on military, and perhaps it might be clearer, first of all, if I rephrase it to ask you whether sniping by your forces was exclusively military on military. Does that help you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Madam Prosecutor, as far as I know, as far as I am aware, judging by the tasks which I issued for sniper fire, and any other fire, not just sniper, to be directed at military targets, not just against troops but also military facilities and so on. Let me not talk more about what can be considered a military target. That was the order that we received from superior commands, and that was the order that I gave. So that would be my answer to your question if that is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, actually in this case, not referring to your trial but this trial, we've received evidence that the larger portion, the preponderance of victims of sniping in Sarajevo were civilians, and that's at T13313, and we've also heard from a demographic expert on the large number of civilians killed and wounded as a result of sniping by forces in your territory. During your time as SRK commander, the demographic evidence is that 900 -- pardon me, 253 civilians were killed by sniping in Bosnian-held territory inside the front lines in Sarajevo, and 1.296 were wounded by sniping, and that's from P4998, page 6 in both languages. So, General, it seems like your last statement is incompatible with the figures that I've just read out, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that it is in any way contradictory. What I said and the figures which you mentioned now, they were mentioned during my trial as well, 253, if that's the number, but these are the figures from Ms. Ewa Tabeau, the Prosecution. No one verified these losses. No one did. And it also says there that the losses are not divided into direct shots and whether the fire was legitimate or not. These were -- these are the overall losses which were established in various ways. So I wouldn't go into that. In two years, if the losses were such among the civilians, I do say that it's much, if the figures are correct. It is a lot, for sure. We have seen here, because we did monitor the losses on the Serbian side, during the direct examination we could see how many civilians were killed by their fire per day. Whether these were all instances of sniper fire, that is again one and the same subject, or whether it's infantry fire, that's always a problem. And as a professional, as an expert, I can tell you that it's difficult to distinguish whether it was sniper fire or ordinary rifle or some other fire. Special expertise is necessary in order to prove that this was sniping activity. If there was any conflict along the confrontation line and infantry fire was opened, she just put it all under sniping activities. So that would be my last answer. And such loss of civilians was unnecessary. Now, whether the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and its forces were to blame, equally other forces were to blame, whether they took the necessary measures that should be taken into account, and both sides should be faced with the problems they created during the war rather than blame just one side. I can see that we are the only ones who stand trial for Sarajevo and sniping. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. No one is accused for the losses among the Serbs in Sarajevo. That is not normal, that everything is fine over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, General, you've actually not explained, as far as I can see, how the figures are not in any way contradictory, but I think what I'd like to do is deal with an issue that you've raised a few times now and it's about the -- a distinction you keep insisting on between sniper fire and ordinary rifle fire, infantry fire. And, General, when you first came in here to testify today, you referred to footnote 711 in paragraph 254 of your appeals judgement, and in that footnote --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In that footnote, the Appellate Chamber makes it clear, General, that the case doesn't require a definition of sniping or proof of specific types of weapons, because you, General, were actually charged with murder and other inhumane acts. So, General, when one of your soldiers shoots a civilian with a gun, it doesn't actually matter whether you call it sniping, does it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, it's not as you present it, the footnote 711, and I would ask for the footnote to be read out here. It's not a long one. Because it explains, first of all, what sniping activity or sniper fire is. It says that it's direct firing from infantry weapons, if I'm not correct [as interpreted]. That's what the footnote says. And then the conclusion is that I'm neither accused nor sentenced. If I'm not accused, then I'm not sentenced. I shouldn't be sentenced for sniping but for murder and inhumane acts. If you are to interpret that further, you would see that I am not accused and sentenced for that and so on and so forth. Let me not interpret the judgement any longer. So we should say clearly what the footnote says.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll do that for the General, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The footnote reads, and I apologise for not uploading it: "The Trial Chamber defined 'sniping' as the 'direct targeting of individuals at a distance using any type of small calibre weapon.'" And that's in the trial judgement at paragraph 184.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't say so. No, no. No. Paragraph 254, footnote 711 says using any infantry weapons. That is the translation I received. If the translation is poor, then I apologise, but I remember quite well what's written there. And I can bring here the Serbian translation here tomorrow if needed, or send it to you, as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we can look into that overnight and get back to you on that tomorrow, General, rather than spending time on it today. So -- but we still didn't -- you still didn't answer my question, and my question was it doesn't actually matter, General, whether -- when one of your soldiers shoots a civilian with a gun, it doesn't matter whether or not you call it sniping, does it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is important if I am accused of sniping activity, and now when we discuss it then it's not important. We have to distinguish between sniping and not sniping. What's a sniper and what's not. It is important. I'm not sure when the figures were presented. The 253 I think relates to the overall losses of both soldiers and civilians who were shot by snipers. But if you say as you do, I can't remember everything now and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go back a little bit. So you're disputing the accuracy of the demographic figures I've read out to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We disputed that during my trial too.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to shooting civilians with a gun, General, it's the same activity which is taking place, isn't it, whether you're using specialised rifles with special ammunition or if it's single shots from ordinary infantry weapons or bursts of fire, it's the same activity, shooting? Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But what is the purpose of that activity? What's the point or the thrust of your question? I don't know. I didn't understand you. I cannot answer you with a proper answer because I haven't sufficiently understood your question. Shooting is shooting, but whether it's shooting or firing from a cannon or a pistol or from a rifle, shooting is shooting if we're talking about shooting, or firing activity to put that in military terms and be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the discussion we're having or that you're raising is just a semantic one, isn't it, General? The word you use in the context of Sarajevo in the context of your evidence doesn't matter. It's just about shooting, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not so. In our language, shooting means shooting which is aimless. You don't have to target anyone. You can shoot into the air, no matter where. That's shooting. And when you aim, then you take aim and then you fire. That's shooting. Or in military terms, it's firing activity. Anyway you want to term it. And shooting is a bit one -- as a term it's imprecise. You can shoot at anything anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At weddings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I find that you're answers are formalistic and you're still not answering my question, so I'll try one more way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think, Ms. Edgerton, you could be clearer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it Ms. Edgerton means targeting civilians. So whether it's by sniper unit or whether it's by ordinary gun by ordinary soldier, it doesn't make any difference. That's the point of Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I -- may I help with the interpretation? As His Excellency Mr. Kwon said should not be interpreted as "shooting" but as "targeting," aiming at civilians, targeting civilians. So -- "gadjanje" [phoen] is the word. Aiming at civilians, targeting civilians, rather than just shooting civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Now the General must have understood. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand it all immediately. It's not a matter of my understanding, Mr. President, but I want to be able to understand in order to properly interpret so that I can answer so there would be no dilemma about my answer, what did I answer, and so that it couldn't be said to me: What you said is not true. I want to tell you what is true and what I know. If I don't know something, I'll tell you so. And here she's asking me, Did you shoot at civilians? Did you target civilians? And I'm saying no, we did not target civilians. There was no ordinary that was issued to target civilians. No, madam and Mr. President. Such an order did not exist. To aim at civilians or to target civilians, there was just an order that it's prohibited to target civilians or aim at civilians and civilian facilities. Such orders do exist. And that I ever issued an order or that someone else ordered that civilians be targeted, I'm not aware of such an order. If it exists, let us look at it and see which fool issued it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want, General --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before I leave this area, General, I'd like to go back to your answer regarding the demographics figures. Now, you said that the demographics figures were not, and I'll find your exact words -- you said that the demographics figures were not contradictory to your assertion that you didn't target civilians, and that's the demographics figures showing 253 civilians killed by sniping and 1.296 wounded. And you haven't explained how they're not -- they don't contradict one another. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've been explaining that all along, but I can repeat some details again and say why they do not contradict. If we taken the entire period, two years of the war, 23 months -- is that correct? 23 months. These were the losses established by Ms. Ewa Tabeau for this entire period, 23 months. So what would be the civilian losses per day if we are to divide the figures? If we use the other analogy how many losses there were on the Serbian side, then if by analogy we also use the fact that there was fighting ongoing all the time, that there were civilians in Dobrinja, for example, where there were the most incidents, where we have six incidents of which President Karadzic stands accused, of all the listed 15, I think that there are 6 there, or Alipasino Polje. We had such a situation, on one floor we have soldiers, on another are civilians, and on the third floor they're mixed, and then when combat occurs there's an exchange of fire, then it's possible that some civilians may perish too. And if we have a front that extends along 65 kilometres, during so many days of combat we will see that it's much, any civilian loss is unnecessary and it is much, but it does happen. Well, that would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ah. So your answer is that civilians killed and wounded by sniping were collateral damage. Is that how we should understand it, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they were all collateral damage, each particular loss should be analysed now, and we should assess whether it was so or not, or whether there was some deliberate targeting. That possibility should not be excluded. There were all kinds of people at the front. All kinds of things happened at the front, Madam Prosecutor. You know, there were people there who, for example, had three of their children killed, and then to control all of them, whether they would take some initiative and do something or not, it's difficult. What I'm saying is that it's normal to expect under such a situation that there would be such collateral damage too. If it's such a long period and so much fighting within Sarajevo on a daily basis in various locations on various fronts, various losses of both soldiers and civilians, then it's possible that some loss of civilians occurs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To move away from sniping, Dr. Karadzic discussed with you also some shelling incidents, and one of them was the incident of the football game in Dobrinja on the 1st of June, 1993, and you discussed this with Dr. Karadzic at transcript page 37367 to 37368. And you talked, in discussing that incident, you said that there was a cease-fire in that period, that close to the place where the incident took place there was an atomic shelter that was supposed to be used by civilians but it was used to shelter soldiers and materiel from recoilless guns, and the incident happened perhaps 150 metres in depth from the confrontation line. So I just want to go over that a little bit now, General, with you. You remember giving that evidence. Now, based on what you've said, there was no fire coming at your forces from the atomic shelter. It was a storage unit; right? That's -- I think that's probably something you could answer with a yes or a no, General. There was no firing coming at your forces from the atomic shelter; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from the shelter, but next to the shelter, yes. But on that day, whether there was fire, whether there were troops or cannons inside on that particular day, I was telling you just my general remarks about that and what I know. If you know something more, please tell me and do ask me. I will answer any question you ask me, because you should take into account what the depth was. I think it was 110 metres, or it could have been 150 metres as you said or as I said, I don't know, but that's it. At 150 metres from the confrontation line, that was where the disposition of the enemy forces was. On one side and on the other as well. There's no dilemma about that. Whether the atomic shelter was closer or not close to the incident itself and so on and so forth, I wouldn't expand that any longer, but I would rather wait for your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, on that day was there fire coming from next to the atomic shelter, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, madam, if I remembered each specific day, then I would be a genius, but I don't know. It's an important date, but I didn't know at all what happened there then. I only received information about that later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right, then. Now, you talked about, as I indicated and you've just spoken about, the position of the confrontation line. You, General, as career officer and an experienced commander, you wouldn't think of placing a mortar on or even near a confrontation line, would you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances I would not, but under such circumstances, there were all kinds of dispositions. Not everything was in accordance with the norms and rules. There were many things that were different from the rules or different from what I would have done. You should know that the army was constituted on both sides from the Territorial Defence, and depending on what everyone had, they would then deploy themselves accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about what you would do. You wouldn't fire a mortar at a target 150 metres away because that would put your own soldiers at risk, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, that is an excellent question. You are thinking along the same lines as me, and I'm glad that this is so. In such a situation it was realistic to expect that that was too close, because the safety zone for 120 mortars, if my memory's correct, was it 120 or 82 millimetres? Because the safety zone is different. The calibres are what the safety zone depends on. But for such calibres, the infantry ones up to 120 millimetres, it has to be at least 200 metres, 200 metres from the location which is targeted. At least. Or 400 metres for bigger calibres around 120 millimetres or more. That is why I agree with you that it wouldn't be normal to fire from a mortar on that line, but if fire was from smaller calibres, then it's possible. The risks were high if they fired from my side. You know that those weapons necessitate corrections also for every instance of firing and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I intervene about the transcript. In line 24, 5, line 78 [as interpreted], the General could explain to us for which calibres is the safety zone 200 metres and for which calibres is it 400 metres because this has been missed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That is the safety zone or security zone. Please interpret it properly. The safety zone. Because it is conditioned by the positions for a charge which are 200 metres from the locations that are targeted by these weapons. The minimum is 200 metres, and for bigger calibres from 120 millimetres upwards, as in this case, the safety zone is around 400 metres, around 400 metres. That was why I agreed with Madam Prosecutor when she noted and stated her expression that that was too close if it was fired from my side, that is to say, the side of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you wouldn't do that. You wouldn't fire a mortar from 150 metres away because of the danger to your own forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, I understand what you're asking, but the interpretation is not very good, so my understanding was that you asked something different. In that situation, it is not permissible to fire a 120-millimetre mortar at a 150-metre distance where my forces are because then I would expose my own forces to that mortar fire. There's another thing. Also, if we have an obstacle, if we have a high-rise building in between, then it is possible to target the area that is shielded by the high-rise because the fragments will not get to our positions. That's possible too but that is very risky.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, General, you certainly wouldn't -- you talked about your own side. You certainly wouldn't fire at your own side at a distance of 150 metres as part of a conspiracy, because people would know that you fired from that close. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I understood what it was you were asking me, because all of that is a bit illogical from the point of view of military terminology and military knowledge, you know. All of this firing that we talked about now. You're asking me whether I would use my mortar that is 150 metres away from the front line; right? Whether I would fire from my mortar. If this is where the line of my forces is, whether from here I would fire 150 metres here? Is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to know if you agree that you would not fire at your own side 150 metres away as part of a conspiracy because people would know that you were doing it, that you were firing from that close.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understand why you're asking me that, because the logic I used was of tactical technical possibilities and the use of forces and resources, but you're asking me about a completely different topic that I really didn't focus on, whether Muslims had targeted themselves. That is how the question was interpreted and that is how I'm interpreting it. So now this mortar that was Muslim here, whether it fired at its own forces and so on. Now, applying that logic of yours that you used to interpret this --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just before you get started --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him -- let him finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry. I just didn't want [sic] to avoid a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood it properly now, what the point of your question is, all you -- although you didn't say that that is it, but now I understand that that is it. Now that you're asking me about that. Certainly it is risky. At any rate, from both sides, but if one runs such a great risk, then that variant is possible, with some difficulty, but it is possible. But with such calibres, it isn't really very convenient.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was whether you would do it.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I would never order anyone to fire at civilians regardless of whether they're my side, the other side. I'd never do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's go back to my question. My question was: Would you agree that you wouldn't fire at your own side from a distance of only 150 metres away as part of a conspiracy because people would know you fired from that close. People would know it. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're putting a hypothetical question to me, and it can be answered in a variety of ways. One must bear in mind that there were mobile mortars in the 1st Corps of the BH Army, so it would stop, fire, and move on momentarily. However, it would have to be a large angle of the mortar, I mean to fire at such close range, you see, because 45 degrees is the biggest range, and then it varies afterwards. So it's the so-called upper group of angles and lower group of angles. I would never do that. I repeat, and if necessary I'll repeat it ten more times, I would never target my own civilians and, on the other hand, from this close range, whether anybody knows whether people are involved in combat, a game, a provocation, I mean I can only speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Under ordinary circumstances, you can hear a mortar being fired 150 metres away, can't you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a long time, you know. I mean -- well, yes, you can hear it. That calibre, yes, you can hear it. Any other mortar calibre would be heard at a 150-metre distance. It could be heard. Even 60 millimetre -- yes, at 150 metres it could be heard, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So everybody would know if you had fired it from that close; right?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether they would know or not know, it would be heard. So those who hear know, and those who do not hear do not know. But we've already said that what I said is important, that at that distance the firing of a shell can be heard. So not when it falls on the target. Because you asked me about the firing, didn't you? That's how I understood it. This firing can be heard at 150 metres regardless of the mortar calibre. That's for sure. Now, whether high-rise buildings may affect this, to a certain degree, but not prevent anyone from hearing it. However, also there's the problem of what is shooting from where and so on and then you cannot distinguish at all what it is that is firing. For instance, if you do not hear a shell being fired, then it is very dangerous because it is certainly flying at you rather than flying above your head or nearby. So much for the fortunes of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But it was a cease-fire that day on the 1st of June, 1993. You even said it in your testimony. At transcript page 37367.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I'm not changing my testimony because certainly there was a cease-fire then. Now, whether from the side the BH Army there was some firing and whether there was a response to that firing and to what degree and so on, these are questions that would have to be looked into once again as regards that day, but certainly there was a cease-fire and that's what I said and if that is what was written in this daily report, it must have been a daily combat report, my daily combat report, I'm sure that's what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if something had been fired 150 metres away at a time of cease-fire, everybody would have heard it. If a mortar had been fired 150 metres away during a time of cease-fire, everybody would have heard it, wouldn't they have, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The question has to be, I think, slightly modified. Everyone who was in the vicinity would have heard it provided they had been of relatively normal hearing and within a reasonable distance. I mean, it can be heard at 150 metres according to the General's evidence. That doesn't mean to say it can be heard at 300 or 400 or 500 metres, so there's going to be a relatively limited group of people that will be able to hear it. General, that must be the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, I'm the one who's supposed to answer so I will say that you fully comprehended what should be answered to this question and I'm so pleased that it is so. So whoever was within this zone of 150 metres heard that or who was not busy. However, if there were other firings, Judge, then you cannot really distinguish from where a shell had been fired and whether it had been fired because there are other sounds that are louder than the firing of that mortar. You have to understand the war and then observation is quite different. It's not simple. It's not that that is the only thing that is happening. We know some of the things that were happening. So as I said, this is your approach to the problem. I as corps commander know some of the truth around Sarajevo, but I do not know everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would like to thank Judge Morrison for his intervention, because I was going to stand up to say exactly the same. I would like a bit more fairness in the way questions are asked, because if you quote passages of Mr. Galic's testimony, you probably noticed that several people said that in Sector Sarajevo we couldn't hear and distinguish between the noises because of other surrounding noises. And trying to trap General Galic with such questions when you know that military observers already established that it was very difficult to establish this specific point is not fair and this is the reason why I've stood up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As to the fairness of the question and conduct of trial, you may leave it to the Chamber, rest assured. Let's continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just want to ask you, General, now about the market-place incident in February 1994. Could you tell us who told you that there were 10 commissions that were unable to establish where the shell came from? Because that's the evidence you gave at transcript page 37444.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one told me about that. I read it in the newspapers, and I know that several UNPROFOR commissions worked and here at my trial it was stated that at least four or five commissions were operating. Now, later, whether there were Muslim ones or, rather, of the 1st Corps of the BH Army or whether it was just these commissions that dealt with it, I did not receive any reports about that with regard to the 5th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And to go back to your evidence at transcript page 37445, you said from the reports you read in respect of this incident, after returning to the corps command you learned that a commission or somebody was established to inspect the units. So, General, what reports did you read after returning to corps command? And who wrote them?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether I had put it that way, that these were reports or statements, or whether I put it some other way, but they made me aware of what was happening then, and then I really did find out what was happening in that area, because it was something that most had become aware of that, myself included. I said that General Gvero was at the airport and he asked for a joint commission to be set up and to explore that. I just heard this, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who did you hear it from, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was actually Gvero that I heard it from.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who was on the commission?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did not understand me. This commission that was supposed to be established was just a commission that was supposed to be established. However, earlier on it had been defined that a joint military commission should be established in such situations. Now, whether this would be at the level of the Main Staff and the staff of the command of the BH Army, the UNPROFOR command that would be headed by the UNPROFOR command for Bosnia-Herzegovina, or whether perhaps a lower-ranking joint military commission should be established that would be at the level of the UNPROFOR Sarajevo Sector, then the 1st Corps of the BH Army and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. So they refused. Actually, the representative of UNPROFOR then, as far as I've heard, the representative of UNPROFOR and the representative of the BH Army refused. They said that this kind of joint commission could not be established that would include Serbs because they could not guarantee -- I haven't finished my thought yet. They could not guarantee the safety of the work of this kind of commission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you said in your testimony that you learned that a commission or somebody was established to inspect the units, that's incorrect. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's a completely different matter. This needs to be looked at separately. If we recall the daily report of the 4th, that we discussed here during the examination-in-chief of the 4th of February, 1994, in this daily report it says that they found out from the media, et cetera, et cetera, that some commission or whatever, they went to subordinate units, they checked this and they established that fire had not been opened, et cetera, et cetera. So then there was some other commission there that toured the area because we had not had information yet, either from UNPROFOR or from anyone else, from where it was assumed that it was possible to fire at the Markale Market, because you have to understand that the Markale Market is in the centre and that it's 3 or 4 kilometres away from the external positions -- or, rather, the positions the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And now just to hit with one single shell that area, that is almost impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was on the commission?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They toured this -- I think there were some representatives. We had a commission that had been established, Colonel Kosovac headed it, headed that commission, and it would be established for every incident. Now, whether he went then or whether some other commission had been established, I cannot say, but they said that they could not establish what had happened. Actually, I said and I was made aware of this detail that they were reviewing the mortars and you could also see the cap on the mortar barrel because there was snow at the time and this was supposed to protect it from the snow, so it could not have been fired if it was snowing. That's something I already said before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But who told you that?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the corps command. That's what they told me when I came. There was this general alert, frankly speaking. The representatives of UNPROFOR were there, representatives of the Supreme Command and the Presidency and so on. So everybody was already working on this case and officers were already being made aware of what had happened and what had not happened and so on, and then later on we know that there were commissions of the United Nations that were working or, rather, of UNPROFOR --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to know, General --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- not --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- one single person or the single person who told you about seeing the cap on the mortar barrel because there was snow at the time. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the command. I cannot remember exactly who told me that in that situation because there were a lot of problems then that had to be resolved regarding that particular incident, because immediately after that, different discussions negotiations followed and so on. Now whether somebody told me at the corps command, I cannot tell you who it was that told me. I'm just telling you who the person was who was supposed to head these commissions and that was Colonel Kosovac. That is what I can tell you. As for the rest, to remember who told me that then, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. So you -- you don't know who went to look at mortars. You don't know who told you about the snow on the mortar. Do you know the date that these people -- no. If I can actually just have a moment. Okay. So, General, you don't know who went to review the mortars; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some commission reviewed them. I don't know who was on the commission, who led it, who commanded it, I don't know. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You don't know who told you what they'd seen, because you've just given that evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've told you already. I've been repeating the same thing for a hundred times.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I know the person who was supposed to be working there. I was not at the command post then but I came later to the command post. And now, this person who had been appointed, I mean, I don't know what the Chief of Staff had ordered then. I did not go into each and every detail so that I can tell you about it now, 20 years later. I don't know. But I am telling you that some commission went there and that is what the daily report says of the 4th and also the 5th, that they went to check. Now, who was on that commission, what they worked on, what they did, where that report is, who was on that commission, I don't know. I cannot remember. I knew it then, but I don't know now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, we're going to go into one area, one last large area for today, that you spent some time on in your testimony in chief, and it's about the question of water for Sarajevo. Dr. Karadzic, in your direct examination, asked you about the water supply from Bistrica and Tilava and other mountain sources such as Moscanica, and whether you ever prevented that kind of water supply from such sources that did not require electricity, and your response, which is at transcript page 37609, was that as far as you know, there was never a manipulation in terms of water supply. There was never any abuse of water supply in order to have someone sanctioned or punished by doing so. It's impossible to stop the flow of water. But, General, in fact, it was possible to stop the flow of water, wasn't it, or at least to ensure it doesn't reach Bosnian-held Sarajevo, because before and during your tour as commander that's exactly what happened. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're asking me, to what extent. You have better information than I do as far as water goes. In principle, I said that is true, that water had not been abused as such, because from Moscanica, Tilava, whatever, I don't know what was done. If that water had been stopped anywhere then -- well, that's mountain water so there would have to be a dam there that would break. I don't know what would have happened to us and the entire 1st Corps of the BH Army and Sarajevo. However, as far as I know, this water had not been abused for any kind of shortage because it takes this natural course from the source that was then in the zone of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and it was supposed to go into the area of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. That is what I know. I know that this water was supplied regularly and that we in Lukavica from time to time did not have water although it passed by us. So we can interpret all of this differently, what happened. I don't know that water supply was obstructed in any way. If you have some information, tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So -- well, your answer to Dr. Karadzic was that as far as you know, there was never a manipulation in terms of water supply, and now you're saying you actually don't know. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's what I said. As far as I know, that's what I said then, that there was no manipulation of water during the war. I repeat again, as far as I know.
