That's what I said a moment ago too. I know quite a bit but I don't know everything. Now, whether somebody manipulated it, I think that that is virtually impossible. Well, perhaps you can prove to me that it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I have a document here I'd like you to have a look at it, actually. It's 65 ter number 24495, and it's a report on war operations and their consequences for the work of the Sarajevo water supply and sewage disposal systems from April 1992 to October 1995. And I just want to take you to a period even before your service as Sarajevo-Romanija Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's English page 28 and B/C/S page 20. And in the B/C/S it's the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we be advised of the origin of the document and the time or the date when it was issued?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we can go back to the first page of the document, and then over to the introduction, which is on page 5 in English, the introduction explains that this is a compilation of contemporaneous reports on the operation of the water supply and sewage disposal system from 1992 right through until 1995. If Dr. Karadzic would like information about the date that it was issued, I would have to check into that and get back to Dr. Karadzic tomorrow. And if Dr. Karadzic objects to using this document now, we can deal with it tomorrow as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance. On page 99, in the contents it reads, "signatures by the members of the working group," but that page, together with 20 others, is missing. If we look at page 3 of the contents and one page -- or, rather, one bullet point but last points to the fact that members of the working group signed the document. However, there are a total of 20 pages missing in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think we have a pretty large translation problem which I'll deal with by the time we come back tomorrow. And thank you to Dr. Karadzic for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Still on the same subject, though, and in relation to Exhibit D3479, and we can have a look at that, it's a Sarajevo-Romanija Corps daily combat report dated 26 November 1992.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can the report please be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. You had a look at this document and said that -- pointed out that it reported the Blazuj transformer station was hit by a 120-millimetre mortar shell which had been fired by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that 4 tonnes of transformer oil leaked, and then you seem to suggest that when the transformer was hit by a shell, it stopped it from functioning and supplying electricity to the city of Sarajevo. But, General, I'd like you to have a look at this document again, and the relevant paragraph is paragraph 1. It's the fourth paragraph down from the top. The document actually doesn't say that the transformer stopped working, does it? That was your own conclusion; right?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, if 4 tonnes of oil leak from the transformer, it can be ignited, but it cannot work, as far as I understand electronics. If you think it can -- I don't think it can.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Apologies to everyone. The question related to this -- was drawn from the document where we had a translation issue. I'll just simply move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I've confused you, General. And finally, General, if we could have a look at D3481, and that's your daily combat report dated 19 June 1993, and it says at point 1, paragraph 1: "The enemy attacked elements of our combat disposition and fired two 82-millimetre shells and rifle grenades on the cargo gate and the power line near Pretis and the power line was damaged and Pretis couldn't work due to the power outage." Now, General, you said about this that this power line runs parallel to the front line and enters Vogosca and then continues toward the centre of Sarajevo, and -- but you didn't have a map to be able to say where those power lines ran. And you were sure that they go to the city centre because one line ran from Hadzici and another from Vogosca and one part from Pale down to the old city. Now, again, this document actually doesn't specify whether this was a power line connecting Pretis to the electricity supply or to the main power line at that feeds the part of central Sarajevo, does it? It doesn't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, this would be a question for an expert. An expert would look at things differently. I'm a soldier. I know about this as much as I had to know about this. I remember when -- where transformer lines went, and if the transformer is damaged in the direction of Vogosca or Pretis, I'm sure that Pretis couldn't work because there was no electricity supply. And when I spoke about various directions, I told you that I remembered that line followed the River Bosna in the direction of Vogosca and from there it forked off towards Hotonj or perhaps it went directly through to the -- to the other part, but I don't know exactly. It went in the direction of the centre because there was not just one single direction of electricity supply for Sarajevo. There were several directions, several sources, the network was the same but one direction was from Visegrad and another one was from Jablanica and Konjica across Mount Igman, and I don't know other thermal power plants supplied Sarajevo. I'm not an expert. Please do not ask me too much about electricity supply because the answers you're going to get from me will leave a lot to be desired.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was just asking, General, because you had answered Dr. Karadzic about that. So now, based on what you've said now, I'm curious. Based on your answer, then, it looks like you actually have no idea whether the power outage at Pretis had anything to do with the electrical situation in Sarajevo, do you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume. When a network is supplied, it is supplied from several directions. How much influence did the Vogosca direction have on Sarajevo? We can only assume. Maybe the power pressure was reduced or limited for a period of time. You have to understand that we are talking about a network. We are not talking about just one line, and that line was interrupted. And as soon as a contact is established in the network, that means that the network is supplied from various sources. This is the way I see things. Maybe I'm not right. I'm not an expert. If you think differently, please tell me so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could begin a new area, but it would I'm sure take longer than the time we have -- ah, no. Sorry, Your Honours. I'm off my stride again. I thought we were -- I didn't realise we had some time to conclude this afternoon. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, not at all. After such a long break, today has been a long day for everybody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was long, yes. Too long for my spine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you need a break, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a general. I'll survive. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, in fact, the supply of not only electricity, water, but also gas to the city was manipulated, and it was in part controlled through your forces. That's the case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no manipulation, as far as I know. If you know something, please tell me. I can explain whether any manipulation was possible. I said on examination-in-chief that Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Muratovic were involved in that, and they also discussed the postal matter. That was another problem. That problem was never discussed, actually, and all postal or mail networks leading to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were interrupted and all that remained was within the sector of the 2nd Corps of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Magnusson, who attended the first round of talks, if you remember, and later on I heard a statement of his, said that the Serbian side was co-operative in that respect and that we always allowed the flow of the bare necessities for the population as much as we could. Again there was war. There was damage to the mains. A shell fell and mains got -- were shattered, so the water could not flow through the pipe. It flew outside of the pipe. That's the way you have to see things. Or if, for example, if a shell fell on the transformer line, the electricity supply was interrupted along that line. Gas could not be stopped because it -- that would result in an explosion. I don't know what kind of fool would have interrupted the supply of gas. I don't know where you would have to go, to what source to interrupt the supply of gas. There were huge amounts of gas being used by both sides. Even trenches were heated by gas through the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, the supply of these things was manipulated at times of political expediency, and I'm going to show you a document. It's P4802, and it's a record made by the Croatian authorities of an intercepted conversation between Dr. Karadzic and a Colonel from the VRS Main Staff which is written here as Milic --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I apologise. I can't see the text. I has to be blown up. I need to be able to read it to be able to comment upon it. Now it's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this is dated 10 August 1993, and, General, that is the eve of the cease-fire that -- the military cease-fire for Bosnia-Herzegovina that was signed by the warring factions. And in this conversation, which takes place at 7.05, just under halfway down the page, Dr. Karadzic orders that Sarajevo is to be given electricity, water, and gas, and says that Serbs are the winners, whereas Alija is a loser who has no chance to threaten them unless the Serbs make a mistake. So, General, this conversation has Dr. Karadzic ordering a member of your Main Staff with the restoration of the electricity, water, and gas to the city of Sarajevo at a time when it was politically expedient, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I am not aware of any such thing. I've not seen this document before. However, if this order was issued, it was impossible to carry out. If the gas was interrupted in the direction of the Muslim side, the same would happen to my side. If I stop the electricity, I stop it for myself, for my side as well. And the same applied to water. I really don't know how this could be drafted. Obviously I am not aware of all the technicalities regarding electricity, water, and the mail. I suppose that the president was like that as well. If these are his words, I don't want to interpret them, but I don't believe that he issued an order to that effect. This may be manipulation. I wouldn't be able to comment. I can only share my observations like I've already had on so many occasions, and I've told you what the position of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was. I don't know if anybody wanted to manipulate, whether there were manipulations unbeknownst to me, whether people wanted things to be different. I don't know. In any case, whatever was going on, it was unbeknownst to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? I would like to say that the General may have been misled by the fact that it was his Main Staff, but it was not his Main Staff. It was not one of his subordinates that I had spoken to. It was somebody else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I would like to say something about that if I may. It says here that from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, which means that it is very clear that this is not my staff. Whether the order arrived at my staff or not, I don't know. I cannot comment upon this because I have not seen it. I don't know what kind of order that is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may. On line 21, Madam Edgerton said "your Main Staff" so that may have misled the witness into believing that that was the staff of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So it's your position, General, that political reasons and political expedience had no effect on the supply of utilities to Sarajevo. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the laws of electronics and physics, this is not easy to implement. In order to apply political manipulations on such a situation. You can see what the front line was like. Where the water and electricity went, if you punish one side you punish the other side as well. I don't know is it the case that President Karadzic punished the Serbs with depriving them of electricity and water? In my view he would never have done that. I know him as much. I don't know why he would have punished his own people with robbing them of electricity and water. This is not within my purview. It was not up to me to know that. And I don't know how my interpretation would help you. I shared with you all I know. I don't know anything else, Madam Prosecutor. If there is anything else that you think I might know, I will gladly answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look please at 65 ter number 25000. And it's a letter from the city Assembly of the Serbian city of Sarajevo, dated 27 September, 1994, and it's addressed to Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, the president of the National Assembly, and the president -- the prime minister of the Republika Srpska. Now, if we can go over to point 9, which is on English pages 4 and 5 and B/C/S page 4, it says: "In the most recent using of Sarajevo for the purpose of raising and lowering tensions in the whole of former Bosnia and Herzegovina (the cutting off of" - if you can go to the next page in English - "electricity, water and gas), about 40.000 households in Serbian Sarajevo have suffered considerable financial damage." And further, it says that: "The Assembly believes that such activities should be carried out with prior consulting and informing of the political organs of the municipalities and the city ..." Now, General, you just said that you didn't see, you didn't know, why Dr. Karadzic might have punished his own people by depriving them of electricity and water, and this document, General, confirms that that's exactly what happened, isn't it? This document sets out clearly that Dr. Karadzic's own people were deprived of utilities at the same time that people in Bosnian-held Sarajevo were deprived. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please show me who signed that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Professor Vojislav Maksimovic, president of the Assembly of Serb Sarajevo signed the document, General.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not have such information. I didn't know that anybody would manipulate with that. I thought that if we didn't have electricity or water there were problems elsewhere. I never thought that somebody would have ordered the utilities to be cut off. I can't tell you anything else. I really did not have information to the effect that somebody was manipulating the situation. Nobody ever issued me an order to cut off electricity or water. That would have been -- well, this is precisely a confirmation of what I have just told you. If you cut off utilities for one people, you do it for the other, the others as well, and it's a huge punishment. This is all I can say. If this is the way to manipulate the situation, then this manipulation is bad, because both sides suffered, both the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the BiH Army, and -- and the people who suffered the most were civilians, on both sides. I really can't believe that manipulation of that sort was carried out. This may have happened due to this mire [phoen] or because of some interruptions towards the source, but for somebody to issue an order to that effect, to manipulate with utilities, I can only you that I've never heard that from anybody. You are the first one who is saying that those were manipulations. I thought that if there was to electricity or water for a certain time, there was a problem somewhere. A commission would come to see where the problem lies, and the situation would be resolved after that. And it was a different issue as to how long the whole situation would last, and it would also depend on the dynamics of combat activities. Did I say enough about this document? Is there anything else you would like to ask me about this document? I don't see what else I could add to what I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this document as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6300, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I have missed something, but I do not see that any blame was allocated for the use on the Serbian side. Maybe Madam Edgerton has noticed that. I would like her to tell me what page is that on. Where does it say that this was manipulation on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General -- sorry. Your Honours, I've read the relevant passage out for the witness and for Dr. Karadzic, and if he has further queries about this document, I think he could take it up in his redirect.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time to adjourn for today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And in response to your query about the time estimate, Your Honour, I can confirm that I will finish tomorrow, no question, and I will aim to finish by the end of the second session tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 8th day of May, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.44 p.m.,
